speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: FRENCH CONSULATES AND CONSULAR AGENTS IN CANADA-OTTAWA LEGATION
speechtext:
In view
of the statement made yesterday by the Prime Minister that he had advised the French minister to take the necessary steps to suspend the operation of French consulates and consular agencies in Canada, I should like to ask the Prime Minister if he does not think that the reasons which he gave apply with equal force to the continuation of the French legation. Secondly, does the French minister continue to enjoy the usual diplomatic immunity in so far as telegraph, telephone, correspondence or other communications with Vichy are concerned?
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING {Prime Minister): In reply to my hon. friend I would say that I do not think that the reasons which I gave with respect ,to the closing of French consulates and consular agencies would apply in equal measure to-the French legation. The day before I gave reasons why it was thought advisable to maintain the diplomatic relations that exist at the present time between France and Canada. So far as the privileges and immunities which the French minister enjoys are concerned, they are the same as those enjoyed by all who hold the position of minister to Canada from another country.
fMr. Mackenzie King.]
The acting leader of the opposition, the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), asked me yesterday whether as a result of the forthcoming suspension of French consulates and consular agencies there would be any consuls and employees of the consulates who were French nationals and who would be obliged to return to France. He asked1 also if Canada had consuls in unoccupied France whose offices would be closed and who would be obliged to return to Canada. I was unable to give my hon. friend the exact information at the time, but I can now give him the following reply to his question.
The various consuls and vice consuls, and some of their employees, are French nationals who came to Canada solely in their official capacity. When a consulate is closed, the official status in Canada of the consular officers and employees is automatically ended and such officers and employees would naturally leave Canada. Consular officials who lived in Canada before their appointment are not in the same category as full-time career officials. Some are British subjects and some are French nationals, but their status as residents of Canada is not affected by the closing of their offices. There are no Canadian government consuls or officials in unoccupied France and therefore no question of any exchange arises.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, May 20, consideration in committee of a resolution to provide sums not exceeding $2,000,000,000 for the year ending March 31, 1943, for granting to his majesty aid for national defence and security-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Vien in the chair.

Mr. O'BRIEN: I understand that the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) expects to be finished in a short time and I wish to assure the committee that it is not my desire under the circumstances to take up a great deal of the time of the committee or of the minister. But in fairness to the constituency I represent and to the province of New Brunswick I feel I should make reference to certain subjects which are of the utmost importance to New Brunswick and to the dominion, in so far as New Brunswick is a unit in the confederation. First of all let me say that I realize fully my responsibility in taking up any of the time of the committee, but I trust I have done so to a minimum since I have had a seat in this chamber.
As a background for my remarks I should like to place on the record part of a resolution passed by the Maritime board of trade at Moncton, New Brunswick, on November 20, 1941. It says in part:
Be it resolved that relative to population and resources, the maritime provinces have made an immense contribution to the war effort in men and money, and whereas the larger portion of expenditure on new' industrial plants is being made in central Canada, thereby threatening to make an acute state of economic dislocation permanent and irreparable, and whereas through lack of this development we are failing to harness a large part of the potential industrial population of these maritime provinces to the war effort, the maritime board of trade earnestly recommends that the government of Canada take immediate steps to alleviate and rectify this unbalanced condition through a process of decentralization of new war industry so that all social and population factors shall receive an equitable opportunity to participate in the industrial life of Canada.
This resolution I regard as background to my remarks, because it comes from the most responsible commercial body in the maritime provinces, representing New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island.
I can understand that in the war effort we must submerge our commercial hopes and desires with due regard to the permanent good of the nation, so that in the most speedy way Hitlerism and all it stands for may be defeated.

But if Canada is to remain a united country of nine provinces, greater consideration must be given to the maritime provinces. We have heard a good deal in days gone by of so-called maritime rights. Unfortunately that movement, I think, was badly handled so that maritime rights developed more or less along the lines, shall I say, of something jocular. I am not so sure that we have any "rights" in the maritimes; in fact, I do not know that any person or any assembly of persons has any particular "rights". I do know positively, however, that we have a great many wrongs, and perhaps that is one and the same thing.
What I mean by wrongs are those things perhaps which one must charge to the march of events since the first conferences on confederation were held in the Provincial building in Charlottetown prior to 1867. Again, some of our troubles are due to things that nature in her providence has failed to place in our province. That is not an unusual thing. Few provinces, indeed few countries in the world, have possession of all the raw materials required to make them a complete economic entity. One important thing we lack in New Brunswick-which province I admit is small geographically, but, after all, the finer things in life should not be overlooked entirely through consideration of might and enormous size, as seems to be the case in this mad age of speed-I refer particularly to water power. Evidently Canada's war effort is primarily based upon large available power resources in close proximity to war industry. While the provinces of Quebec and Ontario have been bountifully endowed by nature with water power, which man has developed, nevertheless, in Ontario particularly, coal is almost completely lacking, and all the coal requirements of that province must come from the maritimes, principally from Nova Scotia. That of course assists the province of Nova Scotia in an economic sense, but it seems to me that in this time, since money has ceased to be the important factor we considered it to be in the so-called days of peace, if not of happiness, a plan could be worked out by which industries requiring coal to develop steam for power could be located in the maritime provinces, and here I speak for Nova Scotia as I do for my native province.
At Grand Lake in the province of New Brunswick there is a steam-developed electrical plant supplying the province through a hookup. It seems to me that that should be further developed at this time. I realize that the answer will be that the electrical machinery required to put in such a development is not available, although one hon. member a day or so ago mentioned that some

War Appropriation-Supplies
used electrical machinery of this sort was available in the United States. Whether that is so I am not prepared to say, but I do think that the Department of Munitions and Supply, in seeking to get supplies, might well be actuated by another motive also, that of trying to build up Canada. This machinery might be found by that department, with a view to a further development in New Brunswick.
Without wishing to be carpingly critical, let me say that the other day I received a reply to a question I put on the order paper asking what was the amount of money provided by the dominion government by way of capital assistance to private industry and to wholly owned government corporations. I asked:
1. What is the total amount of capital assistance given by the Department of Munitions and Supply to (a) private industry, (b) wholly owned government corporations since war was declared?
The answer to that was:
(a)	$498,766,451
(b)	$71,464,857
as at December 31, 1941, for United Kingdom account and January 31, 1942, for Canadian account.
Figuring that out according to the arithmetic table, which so far at least has not been changed by order in council or government regulation, I find that we have received what I might call the ridiculous percentage of [DOT]00019 of .that total for (a) and (b) of $570,231,308. At least New Brunswick has received plenty of zeros. But our people down there cannot consume or live on zeros. Perhaps after many years Euclid has been proved to be correct when he said that a point (or zero) is that which has position but no magnitude. I do think, Mr. Chairman, that these figures illustrate that there is not a consistently conceived national policy prevailing in Canada at the present time. We in this chamber do represent our own constituencies; when we become members of parliament, as I have said on a previous occasion, we lose our personal identity and become a symbol, the member for a particular riding. But in the larger sense the 244 members, not counting Mr. Speaker, endeavour to govern this country as a national entity, and I cannot understand how we can hope to have a united Canada if each province is to be governed by a sort of patchwork system, putting a patch on when pressure develops here, hoping the patch will hold the pressure back until pressure in another location will call for a patch elsewhere. True, the Department of Munitions and Supply cannot be used at this time as a means of promoting social welfare for the present or into the future if
it is going to retard Canada's war effort. But I cannot understand why 500,000 people in the province of New Brunswick and the populations of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island cannot participate in a larger way in Canada's war effort.
In New Brunswick we have some oil shales. This was mentioned yesterday, and the minister explained, rather briefly, I thought, the situation prevailing there. I put a question on the order paper and received a reply. I now wish to state that a lease covering some 10,000 square miles in New Brunswick was made to a company to promote the development of products from that area. This company was primarily engaged in the production of natural gas, and as a result confined itself to sinking shallow wells, the idea being that if deeper borings for oil were made the pressure of the natural gas, in which this company was chiefly concerned, might vanish. But the general welfare of the province suffered as a result, and I am glad to say that I understand within the last few years that lease was cancelled. I was also glad to know, from a statement made by the minister, that he is asking officials of his department to determine to what extent oil may be developed from shales in New Brunswick. As I understand it, the deepest well in the province is down to about 3,500 feet. I believe there are about 126 such wells.
The situation there was somewhat similar to that which prevailed prior to 1936 in the Turner valley, where only shallow wells had been put down. But six years ago very deep wells were sunk, and as a result the Turner valley became one of the bright spots in our .Canadian industrial life, and is proving to-day to be of the utmost importance in, may I say, the preservation of civilization. If such is our objective, and we believe it is, considerations of dollars and cents should vanish completely, and the New Brunswick deposits should be thoroughly investigated and promoted. Nature gave us these resources, and man should put them- to use.
In New Brunswick we also have a coal supply, principally at Grand Lake. The coal deposits in the province have never been developed, although there are, I believe, some thirty outcroppings, appearing in eleven out of the thirteen counties. There again, it seems to me, nature has provided us with something which might be developed.
What I rose to discuss principally was the situation regarding pulpwood in New Brunswick and the maritimes, as this is another commodity which comes under the Minister
War Appropriation-Supplies

of Munitions and Supply. Busy man though he is, it also has been attached to his department, and in turn, of course, a timber controller was appointed, and a deputy controller for pulpwood under the timber controller. I happen to know something of the pulpwood business, because lumber is the product to which I devote my private activities. It is not the first time that I have referred here to the pulpwood situation in New Brunswick. In December, 1940, the Minister of Finance had a resolution before the house regarding tax concessions to be given to pulp and paper companies, upon the theory that they were depressed during the basic period 193639. At that time I said I agreed that business generally should be treated flexibly. Here is a brief quotation from my remarks which appear on page 746 of Hansard of December 6, 1940:
. . . the newsprint industry should be informed that the primary producer of pulpwood, the farmer, is not receiving a sufficient return in view of the increased profits and the much greater returns which evidently the newsprint companies are making to-day.
By "returns" I of course referred to the financial return. At that time, Mr. Chairman, pulpwood was being purchased in the province of Nova Scotia at $7 per cord of 128 feet. Again, as recorded in Hansard of March 18, 1941, and in November, 1941, I was forced to quote from the press references to the pulp and paper companies indicating the enormous earnings they were then making, which in one case increased from 44 cents per share to $4.14; in another case it advanced from 14 cents per share to $6. If these companies were earning at that rate, I submitted, they were in a position to pay more than $7 per cord for pulpwood to the farmer-producer. Nothing was done in the way of appointing a controller. However, as always happens, the law of supply and demand operated, and pulpwood began to acquire in the hands of the primary producer a greater value. Because of some requests, a controller or deputy controller was then appointed. There was a great fanfare of publicity, and we were told that an acute shortage of pulpwood existed in Canada. I could not understand, if that were so, why there was no great demand-and there was no great demand in the province of New Brunswick. In a return brought down on April 28 the following question and answer appears:
5. Is there a serious shortage of pulpwood in Canada?
Answer: No.
If that be so, it seems to me that the appointing of a controller with the embargo which that controller has placed on pulpwood constitute another very serious handicap
[Mr. O'Brien.!
against the people of New Brunswick. After all, if Canada is short of any commodity- it makes no difference what that commodity is-and it is necessary to the winning of the war, it follows, first, that the primary producer should receive a fair and just return for his product, and, second, if it is needed by the nation it should not be allowed to go beyond the boundaries of the nation.
May I, without wishing to become too parochial, cite a case in point? One of my keenest competitors in the Miramichi district received a contract from a mill in the United States which would have brought into the constituency, in United States funds, between $80,000 and $90,000 in a few weeks. That gentleman was refused a permit to ship the total quantity of cordwood mentioned in the contract and was permitted to ship only 500 cords. Yet the Montreal Star referred about a month ago to a further tax concession given to two particularly-named companies because they were extending their plants. One company was bringing in just over 8200,000 in United States exchange in a year. Now, why is this New Brunswick person, who is the keen competitor to whom I refer, not permitted to bring $90,000 in United States money over a short period of time into the constituency of Northumberland for the benefit of the people of that constituency and for the benefit of the foreign exchange control board, while another company was given tax concessions because it would bring in, in the course of a year, approximately double that amount?
That seems to me to be most illogical and not quite fair. Again, to-day we- are facing, we were certainly facing several weeks ago, a most acute shortage in Canada of meat for human consumption. What did happen? In western Canada the farmers held their cattle off the Canadian market, so we are informed, in order that they might receive a higher price by expcrting them to the United States, notwithstanding the fact that there was and still is a ceiling on meat in Canada. It has been reported that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) refused to abide by the ruling of the wartime prices and trade board, on the theory-and I think he was certainly sound in this, morally if not legally-that all through the years the farmers in western Canada had received poor prices for their cattle and are therefore entitled to something more in those particular areas. I say, that is humanly understandable. But if that is proper in western Canada, I should like to know by what line of argument or on what theory the producers of pulpwood in eastern Canada are refused a permit to ship this wood to the United States, there being no shortage in Canada.

War Appropriation-Supplies
I want to make it clear that the ruling, so far as I can find out, is that if an exporter of wood in Canada had been shipping to the United States prior to the placing of this embargo,' that Canadian exporter could go on sending wood to the United States, but not to a new company or to a new purchaser in that country. What logic is behind that? Let me ask this question. How would the Canadian government, the minister himself, individual Canadians feel if we suddenly found placed against our Canadian effort a ruling by the United States government that because a Canadian company had not purchased steel or any other article going into war work that company would not be permitted to buy from a United States manufacturer? To me these things do not in the slightest degree spell consistency or logic. There is a way of sabotaging Canada's war effort indirectly, unconsciously and innocently. We sometimes think of the saboteur as a man who in the [DOT]dead of night creeps into some power plant and, as a culprit, blows up and destroys that property. But in higher places, in broad daylight, I might even use the words through stupidity, certainly through lack of knowledge -that would be a kinder expression-Canada's war effort can be sabotaged. I do not say for a moment that any person is trying deliberately to do these things; but innocently such things can be done. Members of parliament, because of their experience from day to day, are in close contact with what is going on in industry and other lines, and surely they should be in a position to advise the minister, not necessarily here in the house, but at any rate in private in his office, or they could advise his officials, as to what might be done in a practical way to make governing regulations workable. There are so many regulations being passed now, and after all, Canadians are, if I may use the term, free thinkers in these matters; certainly they are of a pioneering spirit, and it seems to me that all these orders and regulations imposed upon business are seriously retarding Canada's war effort.
I believe that members of parliament could be made use of in this respect. They are elected to represent the people in all parts of Canada, and they are in constant touch with every phase of industrial life in the *dominion. Their advice could be given, but instead we are wasting our time in this house wdien we could be devoting our attention to something more useful. Frankly, I wonder why I spend my time in Ottawa. This experience of being a member of the House of Commons has been a great disillusionment to me. True, I realize that we are passing through most strenuous times, but at the
same time the situation demands of us much greater sacrifices and greater energy than we may be able to afford in times of peace. I plead with the minister and the government to recognize members of parliament as human beings possessing some degree of intelligence and devoting their time in parliament to the end that this institution may not, through its present trends, completely vanish as a part of our governmental life. It can happen here; it has happened in other places. A similar governmental institution vanished from Venice, for example, many centuries ago, and all that was heard in pre-war days in the empty senate in Venice was the click of the heels of tourists. Am I to ask myself whether some day tourists will come in here, walk through the building, look at this gorgeous chamber, and say, "Here once democracy functioned, but those who were charged with that democracy failed, so that it is now a museum?"
I repeat, these things can happen here. In my opinion, this institution of parliament is sick and diseased. That disease, that atrophy, is creeping on from day to day, from week to week, unless leadership comes from the government. The things that I mention are not simply the result of my own phobias. I know them and they are presented to me. I am not taking up the time of the house from any desire to embarrass the minister or his department. No. I wish in any way I can to be of service to others, to represent those who have been of great service to.me. I, sir, have been most fortunate; but I must say that down in New Brunswick, one of the oldest provinces in the dominion, a young man starting in life to-day to build up for himself a future, such as my father built for me and passed on to me, has not the chance of the proverbial snowball. It just cannot be done, because business to-day in Canada has become involved in enormous corporations and these corporations are so far-reaching that it is the balance sheet that is ever present whenever human values are to be considered.
Again I plead that this house take unto itself very quickly ,the idea that politics and the seats we hold here are secondary things and that we must preserve our institutions to pass them on to those who will come after us. Let us realize that if we squander these things we shall some day be held greatly responsible. As a case in point, it is a dreadful thing for me to have to say at this moment in Canada, in our present circumstances, that because of the lack of Canadian policy in days of peace, when we thought we could talk ourselves out of depression, if it had not been for the Germans buying pulpwood in eastern Canada
War Appropriation-Supplies

many of our people would have starved. I sat at my desk in my own office and opposite me sat the captain of a German boat. He said, "Mr. O'Brien, what a wonderful country you have here. If we only had this country what would we not do with it!" And I, sir, in great humiliation sat there and listened to that man, knowing that if the Germans had this country they would make it indeed industrially a wonderful country. The river up which his ship sailed for forty miles, from the sea, with 35, 40 and 45 feet of water at the docks, is now completely abandoned. There is not to-day the slightest sign of a ship or a sail or of any animation on that river. Can any other country squander these natural resources and fail to develop them as the governments of Canada down through the years have been doing?
I have spoken about pulpwood, but I have not made any recommendation. I think I should make at least a suggestion. I ask the minister to have his officials seriously consider the lifting of the embargo on pulpwood, until such time as it can be proved beyond the shadow of a doubt that there is a shortage in Canada and that the interests of the Canadian people, not necessarily those of the owners of Canadian pulp mills, are to be served. If that is done then, as in the case of the recent gasoline restrictions, our people, rich and poor, will submit to the very last ounce of endurance. But if there is no shortage in Canada and these people are restricted in their God-given right to earn a livelihood, then I think something is seriously wrong.
I have here a short clipping which rather expresses my experience here in this House of Commons. The article was written by Mr. Bruce Hutchison and appeared in the Victoria Times; I found it extremely interesting. I quote:
One leaves Ottawa with a certain relief, like a man leaving a well-kept hothouse and getting into the fresh air. Ottawa is a hothouse and many of its most attractive growths are orchids, which can survive only in a high temperature and with the greatest care. In fact, Ottawa, speaking in an entirely non-partisan sense, is much too orchidaceous to be the capital of a rough, tough young country like Canada.
It is easy to be absorbed into the official hothouse of Ottawa. Few men survive it. In an intellectual sense they become orchidaceous very quickly and seldom can stand intellectual frost and rain any more.
This is not due to any particular sinfulness of the capital. The House of Commons, in fact, is probably as moral and straight-laced a group of men as you could ask for. There is no management wickedness such as the movies have given Washington; no glorious sirens who lure state secrets from fat old prairie states-

men: no dramas of blackmail and seduction; but rather an intolerable respectability, a dullness which numbs the heart.
That article which I have quoted in part rather expresses my views. I am one of those who desire to serve, and from my seat in this House of Commons I freely offer my assistance to the government. I cannot do more. Again I plead with the minister to make use of the members of this house coming from New Brunswick, irrespective of party. We have ten members here, and I am quite sure those ten will submerge their political leanings at a time like this for the ultimate good of New Brunswick and of Canada. If I can be of any assistance in that respect, even in a small way, I freely offer my services.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I am always glad of the advice of members of parliament; I am always glad to .draw upon their experience, but if the advice is to the effect that we should lift our export restrictions on raw material, I am afraid that would not be very helpful in winning the war. As bon. members know, we have a controlled economy in Canada, and have had for a very considerable time. There is a legal limit to the price which may be paid for pulpwood. There is a legal limit to the price that may be paid for steel, as there is in the case of many other raw materials and finished products. The country to our south, and the various countries to the south of it, have not economies controlled to the same extent that ours is controlled. The price of almost anything is higher in the United States, and higher again in central and south American countries, than it is in Canada. What would be the result if we did not exercise export controls? Almost everything we have in the way of raw materials would be sent abroad as raw materials. For instance, there would be no lumber industry in this country, because the logs would go over the border. There would be no paper industry, because the pulpwood would go over the border. There would be no steel industry, because the pig iron and billet steel would go across the border as such. There would be no munitions industry, because all the copper, nickel and other materials we have would go over the border as such. In other words we would be left as producers of the rawest of raw materials, and our manufacturing industry would cease to exist. We control the prices of our finished products, and of course in order to make those products it is necessary to retain in Canada sufficient raw materials at prices consistent with our whole price structure. Pulpwood is not a munition of war,

War Appropriation-Supplies
as such. By putting it through a paper mill or an explosive plant it can be made into a munition of war. My hon. friend speaks of the export of pulpwood to Germany, which he says saved the economy of New Brunswick. Britain is getting that pulpwood back now in the form of explosives. Many of the bombs dropped on London probably were charged with explosives produced from New Brunswick logs.
Mr. O'BRIEN: I should like to deal with that matter right now. The people of New Brunswick, or certainly the exporters of pulpwood, are being more or less accused of having sacrificed the greater and better things of life for the selfish bank account, and I protest most vigorously against that suggestion. At that time there was never any thought of war. But the minister who just made that statement belonged to a government which permitted exports to go to Japan in time of war to be made into bombs which now are falling upon helpless people, and which before long may be falling on helpless Canadians. Our people in New Brunswick have been subjected to this sort of economy for so many years that it would have been nothing short of ridiculous then to refuse that business from Germany, when the Canadian government of the day was unable to offer them any other relief.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I am glad to hear those cheers. That was a very illuminating explanation, and I am sure everyone is quite convinced that any control over the exports of pulpwood is entirely wrong. However, if I may be allowed to continue until I complete my statement-my hon. friend now having made two speeches, he may permit me to make one-the reason there is control over the export of pulpwood is that there is only so much pulpwood available in Canada. Everyone is allowed to log as much pulpwood as he will or can; there is no restriction on the logging. All we ask is that the needs of Canadian industry for pulpwood be filled first. We impose the same regulation on lumber. We tell the lumber industry to manufacture all the lumber they can. We would like them to manufacture every piece of lumber that can be manufactured, but *before they export to a market where prices are higher they must fill the needs of the Canadian market, at Canadian prices. That is what we say in regard to pulpwood and what we say in regard to any number of raw materials. There are very few materials required in the war economy of Canada that
44561-167J
are allowed to be exported freely. I thought everyone understood that; I am surprised that I must explain it. However, I am very glad to do so, because it seems that the explanation is necessary. There is no restriction whatever on the logging of pulpwood, and every stick may be disposed of.
The reason we ask our manufacturers not to accept new customers in the United States is that we wish to manage our own economy while causing the least possible dislocation in the United States. We take the view that if manufacturers in the United States have been in the habit of coming to Canada for their supplies, we would like to see these customers given a preference when we are disposing of our commodities. But we do not wish our people to take on new customers in the United States because of the dislocation that might be caused in that country due to Canada's domestic regulations.

How then does he justify his statements of a few days ago-
