Mr. O'BRIEN:	Madam Chairman, I
should like to reply to the minister.	I

believe I am in order, since in the meantime other hon. members have made statements. The minister referred unkindly to the people of New Brunswick, presumably exporters, shipping pulpwood to Germany. I wish to state clearly, however, that just as soon as war broke out and the British empire needed pitwood, although we knew nothing about this product in New Brunswick-the sizes required were from 4 to 12 feet in length, with top sizes 2^ to 8 inches-New Brunswick operators immediately entered into the production of pitwood. But one of the large Canadian pulp and paper companies operating in New Brunswick, through a subsidiary, refused to turn their organization into the making of pitwood for the United Kingdom until they were paid a price of $14.80 per cord. At that time, nearly two years ago, pulpwood in Nova Scotia was being bought by a pulp mill at $7 per cord. A cord of pulpwood contains approximately 87 to 90 cubic feet, and weighs approximately 3,000 pounds. Now the price is fixed by the timber controller at $10.
I remember some months ago in this house the_ Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) had a very interesting argument regarding the price paid for hemlock lumber by the Department of Munitions and Supply in Nova Scotia. The minister defended the price of $32 a thousand for hemlock lumber, which is an inferior grade in eastern Canada, and cited the timber controller as his authority for that price. A thousand feet of lumber converted into cubic measure is about 87 cubic feet and it weighs approximately 3,000 pounds.
Here is one branch of government which through the timber controller has said that $32 for hemlock lumber is a fair price for 87 cubic feet; yet another branch of government says that the farmer producing pulpwood shall get only $10 for the same volume by cubic measurement, and the same weight content, for his valuable pulpwood. At the time the timber controller authorized the Minister of National Defence to state that $32 was a fair price for hemlock lumber, the Canadian National Railways, under the guidance of the Minister of Transport, was permitting that organization to buy railway ties for approximately $17.80 a thousand. If these things are consistent, then I do not understand consistency.

Madam Chairman, I should like to call a few points to the minister's attention before he becomes com-

War Appropriation-Supplies
pletely bored. I am sure his patience must be wearing thin. Let me assure him however that that is the price one pays for greatness.
I have been particularly delighted to note the grasp the minister has shown of details in his department. Following him one is filled with amazement because he speaks with freedom on so many phases of the immense undertaking over which he has charge. My purpose this afternoon is not to criticize. I have a number of questions to ask in which a number of people in Toronto and the surrounding area are interested.
I was rather disappointed to hear from the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) that there is no organization in Canada made up of scientists and investigators which is working for the improvement of designs sent here from the old country to be applied to boats we are building in this country. The hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) called attention to this fact during the discussion. I think our war effort would be improved if we had some organization to cheek the specifications laid down in Great Britain for boats and for war equipment to be produced in this country. I am informed that a plant in my riding at the present time is making porthole covers from bronze costing forty cents per pound, whereas the engineer of the plant is reported to have said that the purpose for which these are made could be equally well served by a material costing four cents per pound. This is only one small item, but I feel that there are many items of this nature which could be checked.
Another matter of greater importance to me is in connection with our cargo boats. The minister has thrilled the country with the report of the speed shown in the production of these boats. However, if the minister and his department had deliberately set about to build boats that would serve as good targets for submarines, I doubt if they could have done better than the cargo boat that is being built to-day. These boats are of 10,000 tons, and I am told that they are somewhere near 400 feet in length. They are propelled by reciprocating steam engines weighing 100 pounds per horse-power produced, the engines being placed in the centre of the boat, which necessitates a long tunnel to house the drive shaft. These boats move along at from ten to twelve knots, which is approximately the same speed as the underwater craft. As I say, they make particularly good targets. According to reports published in the United States, in order to replace the ships being sunk on the Atlantic route between Canada and Great Britain it would be necessary to build approximately two ships a day, which is more than we are producing in both Canada and the United States.
I should like to ask the minister if any attempt has been made to improve the design of these cargo boats which bear the precious munitions of war manufactured in this country, which carry the aeroplanes which we make and which are so esesntial to our allies. I have been informed on what I consider to be good authority that small diesel engines are manufactured on this continent, and that these could be arranged in groups on a ship near the stern, thus permitting greater loading capacity and almost doubling the speed. I am told that ships can be built with watertight compartments along the side in which could be loaded grain or other cargo that would absorb moisture and enable the ship to remain afloat long after it was attacked.
I am informed that these boats have practically no armour and carry light guns only, which give them practically no defence against a surface raider. I should like to know if any attempt has been made to change the structure of these ships in order that they may carry heavier guns and be able to defend themselves. This is an important issue in our war effort. I am convinced that Canadian ingenuity and Canadian engineers should be given the opportunity of improving, if possible, upon merchant marine designs which were antiquated long before this war began.
Since we have in the greater Toronto area a number of aeroplane plants, I should like to deal for a moment with the question of aeroplane production. I asked the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Bower) a question about the Martin bomber project at the Malton plant. I think when a project costing well over three quarters of a million dollars and employing hundreds of men for nine months is abandoned without a single ship having been built, we are entitled to a more satisfactory explanation than that given by the minister. I take it that the Minister of Munitions and Supply is informed of this project and can give us an explanation.
I should like to call the minister's attention, as I did the attention of the Minister of National Defence for Air, to the condition of the road running to Malton. When discussing roads running to another munitions plant the minister explained that their condition resulted from the fact that they ran through private property. This road runs through publicly-owned property; it is a publicly-owned road, yet because of the conditions of this road many thousands of man-hours have been lost at the Malton plant. The manager told me
War Appropriation-Supplies

that one of his greatest difficulties was to keep his men. The plant is situated a long way from the centre of Toronto, and the transportation problems are so great and the workers find it so difficult to get to work that they take the first job offered nearer the city. This matter is of such vital importance to the nation that no provincial government or municipal authority should' be allowed to hold up the improvement of this road.
I want to call the minister's attention also to the situation of the plant of Canadian Associated Aircraft Limited. I have a letter from employees indicating that they have been informed that the plant, which has been engaged in the production of Hampden bombers, is to be closed until such time as the neighbouring plant, the National Steel Car company, is in a position to take it over and proceed with the production of Lancaster bombers. Since coming into the house to-day I have received a telegram from the employees of that plant to the effect that they have just been notified that 35 per cent of the employees of the plant are discharged, while the rest .are to be put on part time until such time as the nearby company is able to absorb their labour. There you have a group of workers who are anxious to get on with the job of [DOT]building Hampden bombers. They have written to the department and asked why the production of that particular bomber has been discontinued. The only satisfaction they received

I have a copy of the letter which was sent in reply to the employee who 'wrote- from the official who replied was an inquiry about the writer of the letter, who he was and what his interest was in that plant. The situation is such that unless the men are put to work a group of experienced aircraft production workers will be dispersed, and then there will be a further hold-up of production until the new company find skilled mechanics for the project they have on hand.
I should also like to call the minister's attention to a complaint I have received regarding de Havilland. I am told that that plant is working on a four-engine bomber of English design, most or many of the parts of which must come from England. The hazards of shipping may render the receiving of these parts difficult, or at all events delay may be experienced in their reception, and those who work at that plant are questioning the advisability of that production. I have no doubt the minister has much more knowledge of the situation than these men have, but here are men who are interested in war production and they are anxious to know that the best possible means are being taken to increase our war production. I think the

questions they ask should be answered. The statement which the minister has already made on the work of his department, and the knowledge it has given to the people of this country of the vast ramifications of our war effort, is all to the good. I am simply bringing these questions before the minister in order that he may have an opportunity of clearing up much suspicion and many doubts in the public mind regarding this work.
Turning to the field of construction, I have a letter here signed by an employee of the Massey-Harris plant on Weston Road. He has been employed at that plant for three years, and is a reliable man. He tells me that the plant is very much overstaffed, that the employees are actually getting in one another's way. His suggestion is that the work that is being done at that plant could be done by half the number of people who are now employed. I should like the minister to tell us whether or not that plant is working on a cost-plus contract.
I am also told by the same writer that at that plant skilled workmen are engaged in producing kitchen and office furniture from American whitewood which costs approximately $100 per thousand feet-furniture that could be made from Canadian wood and serve the purpose equally well. The Canadian taxpayers who see these things or hear these things from men working in these plants want to know where their money is going and whether they are really getting value for all the money they are spending on the war.
I am further informed that at the small arms plant at Long Branch, also near York South riding, very expensive building material is being used, material so costly that a building in which it is used should last for fifty years. It may be that it is the intention of the minister or the department that that building should last fifty years. It is possible that they have plans in mind that will thoroughly justify the use of these expensive materials. But you have the public wondering why. They wonder why, in an office building for the air training scheme, we are using cut stone, 7,500 feet of it, I am told, im one building. The people are asking whether that expenditure is warranted.
I have also a few questions for the minister about the fuse-filling plants, one of which is situated in that locality. I am not sure whether the minister's department has any responsibility for contracts placed with United States companies, but he told us the other day that he received orders for material from various ministries and that he places the contracts wherever he can get the material. There are a number of fuse-filling plants in the United States working on the same type

War Appropriation-Supplies
of contract and filling the same type of fuse as the plant at Scarborough and Cherrier Field. These American companies are Exell Foundry, Falls River, Boston; National FireWorks, Elkton, Maryland; and National Munitions, Elrick, Pennsylvania. My information is that the first shipment of 90,000 fuses delivered by National Fire-Works at Elkton-I have reference to fuse 119, mark 4- were rejected by the inspection board of the United Kingdom and Canada. That knowledge is spreading among the workers in these plants. I have been asked to find out whether these are the facts.
I am also informed that the Canadian factories are filling these fuses at about half the rate of the United States plants, and that a very high percentage of the fuses filled at the Scarborough and Cherrier Field plants are rejected.
My attention has also been called to the fact that considerable difficulty has been experienced with workers in structural steel and heavy steel generally, and that many plants have received shipments of steel and found that they had not the skilled help required. The help in the meantime has probably gone to another plant. A foreman in an industry of that kind asked me to suggest, and I pass the suggestion on to the minister, who has probably thought of it already himself, that there be formed a pool of steel workers under the direction of the minister or some official, so that when a plant does receive a shipment of steel, the officials will know immediately where the workers may be found, whence they may be sent immediately to that plant and be available for plants working in the steel industry, in order that there may be no delay through loss of time on that account.
Finally, I would ask the minister if any steps are being taken*in his department to set up a cooperative effort between workers and management. We have received numerous reports from the United States where this cooperation between managers and workers by means of cooperative committees has speeded up production in numerous instances. I understand that the workers' representatives have been asking for a long time that some such committees be set up in the munitions plants and other war industries in Canada. I doubt whether that can be done unless the government itself is prepared to take the initiative and show some leadership in that respect. I think it should be done. Managers and workers alike are interested in production, and given some leadership from the government, it is quite possible that cooperative committees can be set up in our industries which will assist us greatly in our war effort.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Regarding the design of ships, I think it is hardly fair to say Canada is contributing nothing. We have a firm of marine engineers and designers, Messrs. Lambert and German and Mill-to give them some publicity. They have been here for many years; they are very expert; they have designed a large part of the shipping which has been produced in Canadian yards. Mr. Mill is retained permanently by our director of shipbuilding. He has, I think, contributed a good deal to the design of ships which have been built in our shipyards during war time.
My hon. friend referred to the type of 10,000 ton cargo ship we are building to-day and said that it might be greatly improved. I may say that this ship was designed particularly to meet present day war conditions. All the designers in England pooled their ideas to produce the design which came from England, and I might say that in the United States and in Canada that design was accepted with very slight modifications. I understand that the Liberty ship in the United States is slightly, but only very slightly, different from the 10,000 ton freighter which we are building in Canada. Both follow the design which is being used in England for common type cargo ships. The ships which are being built in the three countries are practically of the same design. The reason that it is a slow ship is that all ships to-day travel in convoys, and the speed of even the so-called fast convoy is only about ten knots, so that a ship of eleven and a half or twelve knots is as efficient travelling in a fast convoy as a ship whose speed is five or six knots greater.
Early in the war it was the practice that ships of fifteen knots and over travelled without escort. However, it has been found that losses of ships travelling without escort, even at considerable speeds, are heavier than of ships in convoy. To-day very few freighters, regardless of their speed, travel out of convoy. As a matter of fact, ten knots is a rather high speed for a convoy. I believe that nine knots is more nearly the speed of a fast convoy, and about six knots is the speed of the so-called slow convoy.
Steam is used as a propellent for several reasons. One is that the steam engine is cheaper to construct. Another is that coal is a fuel available everywhere. And of course, in case of damage steam engines are the most easily repaired. Diesel capacity is highly regarded for high-speed passenger ships, but in the freighting trade steam has always been preferred to internal combustion engines.
The story of the Martin bomber is typical of what the aircraft industry is up against in war time. The story is that our air force
War Appropriation-Supplies

ordered the procurement by my department of a considerable number of Martin bombers. It was decided that the Martin bomber should be manufactured in Canada, and arrangements were made to manufacture them at the National Steel Car plant at Malton. The job was put in hand at Malton and a considerable amount of work was done in setting up jigs for that type of manufacture. When the work was nicely under way we received a very urgent demand from Great Britain to arrange in Canada for the manuufacture of a new-type four-engine bomber which was believed to be superior to anything then in combat. Naturally we objected that we had no suitable capacity. We had an emissary come from England to urge the necessity of developing this type of production, and after consultation with the air force we finally decided that the urgency and the needs of Britain were such that we would be well advised to change over from the Martin bomber to the British type. The British-type bomber is on the secret list, and it is not permissible to mention the name.
Britain had an order of Martin bombers in the United States, and these bombers for Britain were the first off the production line in the United States. To compensate us, or at least to ensure the procurement of the Martin bomber for our own air force, we were promised the first bombers off the production line for British account. The understanding was that there would be an exchange of dollar for dollar: we would get the Martin bombers from the United States through Great Britain and we would credit Great Britain with the cost of the Martin bombers in the United States against the British-type four-engine bomber in our plant. The cost of tooling was included as part of the amount for which we were to receive compensation in the form of Martin bombers from the United States. There was no monetary loss to Canada on tooling, but of course there was a dislocation there, which has been unfortunate. However, the Anson project was close to production at that time or perhaps had started production. We put a very considerable number of Anson bombers into the plant, and there was actually very little dislocation of labour through the change in arrangements.
I might say that that sort of thing is an everyday incident in the aircraft industry. Unfortunately it is not possible to take a pre-war type of plane and continue to manufacture it indefinitely, for the reason that the art of building fighting planes advances as conditions of combat change. At the beginning of the war the Hurricane was

perhaps the plane that saved England, but to-day it is not suitable for fighting over England because the fighting takes place at altitudes which the Hurricane cannot reach, so that other types are used there. The Hurricanes we are making at the present time are sent to other areas where different conditions apply. From time to time we have had in almost every type of production radical modifications of design which have necessitated interrupting production and introducing changes into the plane, with a good deal of loss of production and slacking off of employment.
The road to Malton is a subject about which I have heard a good deal. As hon. members are aware, the building of highways is not a matter for the federal government. The provincial government, cities and counties are responsible for the building and maintenance of highways with the limited exception of the Trans-Canada highway in which the dominion takes an interest. We have sponsored improvements in the road from Toronto to Malton and have made a gratis contribution of a considerable proportion of the cost of building the road. That contribution has been paid in cash to the provincial government. The sub-grade of the new road is built. We are aware that the road is in bad condition and are making proper representations to the provincial government. I am hopeful that the governments concerned will take action shortly to improve that situation, but it is not a matter in which the federal government can go further than it has already gone.
The matter of Hampden bombers is as my hon. friend states. The plant alongside the National Steel Car plant was assembling Hampden bombers, and the National Steel Car plant was building components of Hampden bombers. That bomber is no longer of sufficient value as a fighting machine ,to be useful in the war, and production in this country has been suspended. The production of the four-engine bombers, to which I previously referred, will supersede that work in the plants formerly operated by the Associated Aircraft companies. This plant will become an annex of the National Steel Car plant. I doubt whether there is any great interruption in employment. As a matter of fact the National Steel Car plant has been, I understand, short of aeroplane mechanics for some time. I rather imagine the men will be absorbed by the plant in Toronto and that the men in Montreal will be absorbed into overhaul work. In any event anyone who calls himself an aeroplane mechanic will have no difficulty obtaining employment in any of

War Appropriation-Supplies
the various plants in Toronto-the National Steel Car, de Havilland, Massey-Harris and one or two others. No man in the aircraft industry will have any difficulty in being reabsorbed immediately into the aircraft industry even though he must leave the plant in which he is working at the present time.
My hon. friend spoke of the de Havilland plant and criticized the type of plane being built there. I hardly think that his statement, that a great number of parts must come from England, is correct. It might have been true with regard to a few initial planes, but my understanding is that the new plane being produced by de Havilland will be an allCanadian product except for the engine. Here again we are building a very modern British plane. It is also on the secret list. We think it marks a definite advance in the type of plane to be built in Canada. It is quite fast, well armed, and capable of flying the Atlantic. It is equipped with twin engines, not four engines, and should be one of the most useful planes in the war. We undertook the construction of this particular plane because we were urged to do so by Great Britain. They felt it highly desirable to have a Canadian source of supply for this aeroplane. My hon. friend spoke of Massey-Harris as manufacturing furniture. I was not aware that Massey-Harris manufactured furniture.

Furniture from
American wood at $100 a thousand.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I was not aware that they
manufactured furniture and I am sure it is not for our account.
My report is that the employees there were engaged in making kitchen and office furniture from American wood at $100 a thousand.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I suggest that my hon. friend may have another plant in mind. I would not be dogmatic about it, but I have never heard of this company manufacturing furniture. Certainly I doubt that they are manufacturing furniture for the Canadian government. It is my information that very little wood from the United States is imported into Canada in connection with the furniture business. However, I am not competent to deal with this question without obtaining more information.
In the matter of small arms, this is a government arsenal for the manufacture of rifles and sub-machine guns. The number of employees per square foot at the plant is very high as manufacturing plants go. To afford employment of that kind it is necessary to have an air-conditioned plant, the best lighting, and conditions that cannot very well be
maintained in a temporary building. I am familiar with the type of construction at Small Arms, and I hardly think it is extravagant considering the extensive use made of floor space. Those familiar with manufacturing will agree that the cost of building is reasonable in proportion to the output. The monthly output valued in dollars from that plant is quite high in comparison with the cost of the plant.
I appreciate the spirit in which my hon. friend has given the information, and I hope I have covered the points he raised. If not, I shall be glad to amplify what I have said.
Can the minister give us some information in reference to the telegram I left with him?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) sent me a telegram stating that 35 per cent of the employees of Canadian Associated Aircraft at Malton would be discharged in three weeks.
Signed by some of the workers' committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Yes. That is very likely correct. This is the plant which was formerly making Hampden bombers, but I feel sure the workers will be absorbed in the adjoining operation or in the de Havilland or Massey-Harris plant.	_
Will the minister give some information on the question I raised with regard to the fuse plants?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: In regard to the fuse plants, we did buy a few fuses before our plants came into production. We got them from a British order in the United States. I daresay there were some rejects, but if there were they were not paid for. They were purchased subject to inspection. I believe the record for fuse filling and small arms ammunition is very much better in Canada than in the United States. At the moment we are obtaining no fuses from the United States; as a matter of fact we are shipping filled fuses to the United States. Everything I learn about the fuse-filling operation at Scarboro leads me to believe that it is a very efficient operation. I know that the costs are good, because we have no difficulty in disposing of the fuses outside the country. I believe the operation is very efficient as to both quality of ammunition and cost.

The minister has dealt with Canadian Associated Aircraft Limited, the employees of which apparently sent quite a number of telegrams to members of the house this afternoon in regard to the closing of the plant and their discharge from employment. From time to time letters have
War Appropriation-Supplies

been received by hon. members in regard to conditions in various aircraft factories in Canada. Within the last day or so I received one such letter, and I think I should mention the name of the plant. I refer to the Noorduyn factory at Cartierville, Quebec. In that factory are a thousand workers, many of whom, according to the information I have received, are idle part of their time because of a shortage of materials. That is something which requires explanation. It is all very well to say that these things are just gossip, but the fact remains that not only in this case but in the case of the plant at Malton there are substantial grounds of complaint.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Did I say it was gossip? M3' hon. friend has given me a specific case.
I am dealing with a specific case.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Do not put words in my mouth. I have not said ans'thing.

I have heard that expression used by the minister on several occasions when such matters were mentioned, but I hope he will not regard this as gossip.
With regard to the Noorduyn .factory, is it a fact that those employed there are idle during some part of their working time because of a shortage of materials? Is it a fact that there has been a shortage of materials? I think there would be a great deal less recrimination in regard to this subject if the minister would place before the committee' such surveys as he has made, which will set forth an>- shortages that have been found and any delays that have resulted therefrom, together with the number of men who have been kept idle due to the fact that there has been any shortage of materials. As far as the aircraft production in December last is concerned, there must have been a decline; otherwise a director of morale would not have been appointed, his duties being to increase aircraft production. I think the committee is entitled to know the circumstances connected with his appointment, including any surveys that were made leading up to the appointment of such an official. My information is that not only was such an official appointed-and I am not now dealing with the circumstances connected with his appointment-but two journals, one in English and one in French were turned out for circulation among the aircraft workers. Is it a fact that such journals were published and circulated among the workers? If so, was the cost met by the government, or was it indirectly financed as overhead? What in general were [Mr. Diefenbaker.J
the circumstances that impelled the director of aircraft production to undertake a morale building campaign?
According to the evidence that was given before the Truman committee in the United States, which went into the matter very fully, there was a hold-up in aircraft production, for which the committee found several reasons. The first was that too much red tape held up production. Is that one of the reasons in Canada? The next reason was that there were too many changes in specifications, with a lack of standardization in combat and bomber planes. The explanation given to-day by the minister in regard to the change from Martin bombers to four-engine bombers was, I thought, very reasonable. Explanations like that clarify the situation; recriminations do not. Is it a fact that there have been too many changes in specifications in Canada? Have we yet arrived at a point where there is uniformity as great as can be secured in view of changing conditions and the exigencies of war?
I would also ask the minister what plans are being made for the production of aircraft engines in Canada. Is not difficulty being experienced in securing aeroplane engines in the United States, now that that country is in the war? The Truman committee also found that there were hold-ups because of the action of certain organizations which interfered with labour engaged in the production of aeroplanes. Has that been the case in Canada? I do not think so. I believe labour has cooperated well, but if it has not, let us have the particulars. Let us know why production is not what was expected. Have any manufacturers, producers or distributors of supplies been negligent in furnishing the aeroplane factories with necessary supplies? Has their neglect resulted in hold-ups in the various factories? If so, have these men been punished? What has been done in order to accelerate proper distribution on their part?
After taking evidence over a long period of time the Truman committee came to certain conclusions, and acted thereon. That was last January, and as a result aircraft production in the United States has greatly increased. So great was this increase that according to a recent authoritative statement, the United States is producing more aeroplanes than Germany. I ask the minister: Has there been an increase in aeroplane production in Canada since the appointment of a director of morale? Does he find that there are wide-spread shortages? These are things which, if explained, may very well go a long way toward explaining the situation which apparently exists in a number of aircraft plants throughout the dominion to-day.

War Appropriation-Supplies
In November, 1940, when the minister first enunciated in this house his scheme of giving financial assistance to industry, he told us he had plans for this industry after the war. The other day he told us that some $380,000,000 had been advanced to industry. The Truman committee looked into the matter of advances to industry in the United' States; they wanted to know what were the plans of the government for the post-war period, in connection with the industries so financed by the government. The dominion government has put millions of dollars into private plants by way of subsidy or capital assistance. Is it the intention that after the war these plants shall compete with private industry?
In -November, 1940, the minister said he had a post-war plan for these plants. What are the plans or what is the nature of the contracts he has entered into with these private industries, and the general purport of the government's plans for their utilization after the war? According to the evidence given before the committee in the United States, the general plan in that country is that private industry to-day operating government plants to which advances have been made are in the position where they shall have priority after the war in the leasing of those plants, and their continuance in civil production.
I would ask the minister frankly to set out the situation with regard to his difficulties in the aeroplane industry. If he places the matter fairly before us, we will give him our cooperation. We are not asking for particulars as to amounts or as -to production in any one factory, because to furnish such information may cause harm. But we want to know something more than mere generalizations in connection with production of aircraft. We want to know whether all is well and, if all is not well, what can be or is being done to accelerate production.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I shall surprise my hon. friend by answering this simple question with a simple answer. He asked if there was a shortage of material at Noorduyns, and I will say, yes, there is, and surprise him very much.
No; that is being frank; we want that.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I was going to say that there is a temporary shortage of aluminum forgings at Noorduyns.

How long has it
continued?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
It has been temporary. It has affected production for about a month, and we think we are catching up with it fairly quickly. Production at Noorduyns has been stepping up very fast indeed.
I would point out that an aeroplane plant such as Noorduyns is really an assembly plant.
It assembles the product made by a great many other plants across Canada. If one of those plants gets out of step, the assembly line is closed down. When we are expanding industry as rapidly as we have-and I said the other day that the aeroplane industry had expanded fortyfold in the last two years- it is, in my experience, impossible always to keep a balance. We may be short of labour or materials at one point; for instance, in the Noorduyn plant we are temporarily short of aluminum castings. However, I do not think anyone has been laid off entirely on that account, although some of the staff may have been put on shorter hours. Instead of working overtime they have been working regular hours, or perhaps curtailed hours. I do not know how it can always be kept in balance. As I said before, a plant, if it is fully manned and fully machined, and with an unlimited rate of output, can be streamlined so that the product comes through evenly every day. But I do not think one could achieve that in the aeroplane business to-day. These temporary upsets or shortages of one kind and another-labour	and material-do	occur
from time to time. That is why the production figures for various months are uneven, and they are bound to be uneven. However, the industry as a whole is making tremendous strides.
The hon. member has asked why a director of morale is necessary. I suggest to him that when 2,000 men come in from the farms and the cities every month, a little help in that direction is necessary to enable those men to be absorbed into industry. I think morale building has had a good effect. Just how it has affected the output of planes I do not know, but I presume it has not done any harm. I would think, too, that it has done some good because the output of planes has risen from week to week, and at this stage of our programme has reached a very healthy figure, especially when we remember that three of our plants are still tooling, and not producing.
I must say that I have not given a great deal of thought to the disposal of our plants after the war. I should like to get a little further along with the war before giving my attention to this. As I said earlier, capital assistance to industry in the form of plant and equipment is retained in the ownership of the
War Appropriation-Supplies

crown. That is, the product of the expenditure remains in the ownership of the crown. When we build a plant, we own the land on which it stands. When we put machines in, we own them. As far as the use of plants built by capital expenditure is concerned, all I can say is that everything is under rigid control. When the war is over, we can do what we like with these plants. We can turn the key in the door, if we wish, and shrink an industry back to its pre-war size. Or, if circumstances warrant it, we can use the addition to a plant for any type of production we may wish.
Very few commitments have been made. Commitments have been made only where secret processes have been used, and in that event we have given the firm which provided the process and supervised the building of the plant the opportunity of first refusal, in the event of the government deciding to sell. This is the only commitment we have made in connection with any plant built with public moneys. In other words, a plant could not be sold to a competitor without our first having offered it to the firm which designed, built and supervised it, and whose process we used without cost. In that way the plant would not pass into the hands of a competitor without first being offered to the firm in question which had built the plant.
At the same price.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Yes, refusal at the bid price.

On Thursday last, speaking of this morale-building campaign, the minister said, as reported at page 2451 of Hansard:
I do not believe in this kind of propaganda in an industry. However, it was represented to me that the industry decided this was a desirable thing to do.
I am at a loss to understand whose policy prevails in the department, whether it is the policy which the minister believes to be the correct one, or the policy put forth by the director general of aircraft production. In that regard also, when the letter first came before the house last Thursday the minister said that when he learned the circumstances he stopped the charging to overhead of any contribution to this morale-building campaign. If the morale-building campaign would help the production of more aeroplanes, which we so badly need, then why is it not just as legitimate a charge against operations as labour or material costs? I fail to understand why the minister at that time had Mr. Bell's suggestion cancelled. What is the position to-day?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: As the hon. member knows, by unanimous vote the industry asked that the campaign be continued. My reply was that if the industry itself wished to continue the campaign, it was at liberty to do so. But there were several objections to the letter, the chief of which was the suggestion that printing be diverted, as a means of compensation. I took strong objection to that. I took objection, too, to an officer of my department asking an industry to contribute money for any purpose whatsoever. If the industry had started a morale-building campaign within the industry, it would have been a legitimate undertaking. My objection was to the letter, not to what was done. There are certain rules of costing which provide for the payment of certain personnel. The director of personnel is a legitimate employee and if he wishes to conduct a morale-building campaign and associate himself in doing so with other directors of personnel, that would be legitimate. My objection was to an officer of my department appointing a man and asking the industry to pay him. If we appointed the man we should pay him.

I quite appreciate that, but the minister was most definite on Thursday last, and I think again on Friday. On Thursday last, as reported on page 2451 of Hansard, he said:
I also made sure that the payments would not become an element of overhead cost on the part of any of the subscribers.
While I agree that it was outside the functions of the director-general of aircraft production to organize this campaign, apparently without very much knowledge on the part of some of the constituent companies, nevertheless I do not see the difference between charging it to the cost of operations when carried on by the director of personnel of one company, and having an association of aircraft producers get together for this purpose and hiring a man to do the job for the whole industry. I do not yet understand if the function was legitimate. If the manner of doing it was not reprehensible, I cannot understand why there should be the slightest objection to charging the cost to operations. The minister was quite sensitive to it at that time; but if it is now being carried on with his endorsation, or at least with his consent, by an association or an officer who is not a direct employee of any one company, I cannot understand why it should not be a proper charge against the operations of the various companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
The collections made at the request of my director-general were not a

War Appropriation-Supplies
legitimate charge in my opinion, and I made sure that they were not so regarded. The rules as to what are legitimate manufacturing costs are laid down very exactly and agreed upon between my own officers, the treasury and the auditor general. If personnel work can be carried on within the four walls of these rules, no doubt it will be carried on. I did not wish to have funds Taised at the request of my director-general for any purpose whatever and have those funds included in costs, and I took steps to see that that particular fund was paid for by those who subscribed and not by the government.

Was there an arrangement with the treasury contained in that
letter?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I could find no evidence, and my colleague could find none.

In effect the resolution now before the committee is a $2,000,000,000 item in the estimates, and I should like to ask the minister a few questions about a matter, the expenditures for which will probably come within the vote to be based upon this resolution. Is it the intention of the government to put Trans-Canada Air Lines on the route from Vancouver and Edmonton to the Yukon and Alaska in competition with planes now being operated over that route? Are airports for this purpose to be built by the government to constitute a route in addition to the route now in use? Does the minister consider that the present temporary abnormal volume of business due to the construction of the Alaska highway will continue? In normal times the planes now operating this route are able to carry all the business offered. What is the estimated cost of putting the government air line on this route?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Trans-Canada Air Lines is owned by Canadian National Railways, and reports to me at the moment because I am Acting Minister of Transport. I am not in very close touch with the company at the moment. The airfields on the route to Alaska are being built to provide an air route, but we are not going to duplicate. Any aeroplanes using this route will use the fields now being built.

The government is
building those fields?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Yes; just as it has built all the fields along Trans-Canada. The purpose of Trans-Canada Air Lines is to operate a
mainline service from coast to coast and certain international routes. Trans-Canada is operating certain international routes to the south, and it was the intention that it would operate any international route to Alaska and northward. Another company has been operating in this area for some time, and I cannot say just what will be the future policy. It will depend upon the wishes of Trans-Canada Air Lines and the decision of the board of transport commissioners which has jurisdiction over all air service routes in Canada. The decision is not likely to lie with me unless I happen to be Acting Minister of Transport at the critical time, which is unlikely. I do not remember my hon. friend's other question.

I asked the estimated cost of putting the government air line on that route. I am asking this question because up to the present time the transport commission have taken great care, and properly so, to prevent any overlapping of aeroplane services in Canada. They decide whether an established service is sufficient and, if it is, they will not allow another service to go in. As I see it, this is going to be overlapping of a most serious nature.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: The only recompense that any company using this route would get from the government would be payment for carrying the mails. The company operating there now is being paid for carrying the mails. If Trans-Canada went into this territory, the only recompense it would get from the government would be payment for carrying the mails. I may say that the Post Office Department has always protected the future position of Trans-Canada as the company to carry the mails on this route. The present contract is a month to month contract, and there have been warnings issued at all stages that eventually Trans-Canada will probably operate on the route. There will be no question of competing lines; if Trans-Canada goes in. the other line must go out.

Will the minister consider issuing permits to pulpwood dealers selling to kraft mills in the United States who are manufacturing war material? These mills were not in operation before the war and are now denied permits because they were not purchasing pulpwood in Canada at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I assume they can find sources of supply in the United States. If the production of pulpwood in Canada extends beyond all previous figures so that it can supply the needs of Canada plus the former purchases by all customers, I have no doubt the timber controller will consider applications for permission to take on new customers.
War Appropriation-Supplies
The newsprint mills have had no trouble in getting permission, but these new mills which are manufacturing war materials are denied permits. In my opinion these mills should have preference.

I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Northumberland, New Brunswick (Mr. O'Brien) who, in a forceful, clear and logical manner, presented the case of what he described as the forgotten province.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: We have now passed to the war of the provinces.

Coming from a province which is in that category industrially, I think I can justify an intrusion upon this debate even at this late hour. I was also interested in his conversation with the German merchant who called at his office some time in 1936. In 1933 the world's grain show was held at Regina and that exhibition was attended by representatives of all the grain producing countries of the world, including Germany. The representative in attendance from Germany had visited all parts of Canada before coming to Regina, and after he had been in that city for a day or two he was asked to give a summary of his impressions of what he had seen and of his experiences. He readily consented, and said that it could be given in two words-"waste" and "space." That description has constantly come to the minds of many Canadians and suggests the thought as to whether or not at this critical time we are making a maximum use of our resources, both natural and man-power.
Recently, owing to the courtesy and consideration of the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Cote), I had the privilege of visiting a couple of munitions plants in the city of Montreal, and were this an earlier stage of the debate I would have been glad to portray what I saw in those two plants. But since being there, I have seen the edition of Maclean's of May 15, and I want to congratulate the publishers of that magazine upon that particular issue. It contains a description of certain parts of Canada's war effort. It describes it graphically and dramatically and gives to the Minister of Munitions and Supply a great deal of credit for what has been accomplished in a very short time. After reading the account of Canada's development in the last two and a half years, and after having seen what I have seen, one can readily understand how it is and why it is that the universities of this country are conferring degrees upon the hon. gentleman in recognition of his accomplishments for Canada and the empire, and I personally con-

gratulate the minister upon being honoured by one of the most eminent of Canadian universities.
Arising out of my visit to Montreal I should like to bring to the attention of the minister and of the committee three or four matters. First, the plant utilized by Defence Industries Limited at Verdun was in use in the last war. I believe it was built by the British government, and following the last war it was used, prior to eighteen months or two years ago, by the Dominion Textile company as their manu-turing plant. What I draw from that is that plants constructed during this war may have and should have a post-war use, and this plant did have a post-war use and was readily converted to the needs of the nation when the occasion arose.
The next point is that of the four men I first met on entering the plant three were from my own city of Regina and the fourth was from Estevan, Saskatchewan, which is an indication of the migration from the prairie provinces to eastern Canada and of the part our people from the prairies are taking in industry.
Apart from the tremendous production in that plant, I think what interested me most was that part of the plant devoted to the manufacture of machine tools, and I was informed that they were manufacturing right in the plant, in the building itself, all the machine tools they required.
The next matter that interested me was a delicately constructed balance which weighed the cartridges after they had been inspected, automatically eliminating those that were underweight, or overweight, and sending down another chute those that were of the proper weight. That machine was constructed by the Bata Shoe company, an institution which has come into this country within the last four or five years, and is an indication of what Canada has drawn from troubled Europe in the way of industrial development and of what can be-developed in the future.
On this occasion I had the privilege of hearing the Hon. Charles A. Dunning, who-is the chairman of the board of .Wartime Industries. Hon. gentlemen will be glad to know that the Hon. Mr. Dunning is gradually recovering a measure of good health, and he had not been speaking very long before he exhibited much of that old-time vigour which we knew so well on the floor of this house. Mr. Dunning was responsible for this statement, and I do not think in repeating it here I am breaking any of his confidences or imposing on the restrictions laid down by the minister himself with regard to quantitative production. Mr. Dunning stated that the plants of Defence Industries were now pro-

War Appropriation-Supplies
during more ammunition every month than was produced by the whole of Canada in the last war, and I understand that at the conclusion of the last war Canada was producing approximately 55 per cent of all the ammunition used by the allies.
While I do not intend to elaborate on what I saw at the two Montreal plants, I do wish to make a more detailed reference to a plant in Regina, my home city. That plant up to the 15th of August last was operating an assembly line for General Motors and employing between five and six hundred men. During each one of its productive years it turned out approximately 10,000 motor units. About the 15th of August, they started clearing out the assembly line and to acquire and install new machinery. Much of that machinery had been installed by the first of the year and production started. The plant is not fully equipped yet. When it is, it will employ approximately 1,000 men, and at the present time there are between six and seven hundred men engaged there. The plant is manufacturing the most modern anti-tank gun that mechanical science has yet produced, and those guns are being turned out every day in the Regina plant and have been turned out for a considerable time. I saw those guns boxed and labelled ready for shipment to a far distant point.
I have always felt-and I am glad to have some confirmation of my ideas in that regard -that it is wiser and safer, and costs less in the long run, for industry to be taken to labour rather than for labour to be removed to industry. Recently there was a conference of national war labour leaders in the city of Ottawa, and on his return to Saskatchewan, Hon. R. J. M. Parker, minister in charge of municipal affairs, said this, in summary of what occurred at the meeting:
Mr. Humphrey Mitchell, federal Minister of Labour, also dealt with labour conditions in the dominion and suggested that the proper policy to follow with respect to the employment of people was to take the work to the people rather than to transfer large numbers to the work. Such a policy might have averted the exodus of people from Saskatchewan in recent years, had industry been established here.
That seems to me to be a very wise policy, and one that will avoid many of the difficulties which undoubtedly will arise in the post-war period.
When General McNaughton was here I had a short conversation with him during which he outlined his experiences in going through one of the large industrial plants in eastern Canada. In going through plants he engaged the foremen in conversation and ascertained what their duties were and where they came
from. Himself a Saskatchewan man, he was proud of the fact that eight out of twelve foremen with whom he conversed in one plant came from that province. That emphasizes the migration of skilled labour from our province to eastern Canada. It is established by the fact that since 1936 Saskatchewan has lost 42,000 people, to say nothing of the natural increase which has not been tabulated during that period.
Mr. Little has ordered a new registration of unemployed. Every unemployed man between sixteen and sixty-nine years of age is required to register. I have no quarrel with that order; I think it is as it should be. But when the unemployed are registered in Saskatchewan, what is Mr. Little's intention? Is it his intention to move those unemployed persons to industries in the eastern provinces, or will he recognize as a principle that which his minister enunciated, namely that it is better to take industry to labour rather than the reverse?
Recently the teachers of my own city sent me a communication which to a certain extent applies to the teachers of the rest of the province. They are anxious to know where they can obtain employment for the two months of their holidays, because they wish to devote their leisure time to the war effort. It seems to me that in view of these facts-I am not censuring the Minister of Munitions and Supply, for I know it is his duty and responsibility to get production, and get it in the shortest period possible-there might be greater collaboration by the Minister of National War Services and the Minister of Labour in setting up war industries which will impose a minimum of trouble in post-war years.
The other evening I referred to the coal deposits in Saskatchewan and expressed the opinion that they should be converted to national use at this time. That thought was emphasized by a recent visit of Mr. Jeckell to western Canada. While there, he consulted authorities in Manitoba concerning the development of 100,000 horse-power of electrical energy, and indicated an intention, should it be found, of building a $40,000,000 aluminum plant. The authorities in Manitoba could not provide the necessary power, and his investigations proceeded no further. I suggest that consideration should have been given to the development of power at the lignite coal fields in Saskatchewan. Much has been said at different times with reference to the bits-and-pieces policy. The trouble in that regard is not peculiar to the Dominion of Canada but obtains also in the United States. I noticed in the issue of PM for April 13 last that that magazine had financed a delegation of idle owners of machine shops and workers to Washington for the purpose of making representations to the authorities there. The reason that PM gave for undertaking that responsibility was this .statement:
Every idle machine, every idle worker, is a national scandal at this date in American history; and to ask this question-Why 85 per cent of the hundred billion dollar war contracts were awarded to only 350 corporations while the rest were spread thin over 186,000 small manufacturers. And later received the answer quite frankly-that limited inspection and clerical facilities made it easier for the government to dump the orders into the hoppers of General Motors, Remington Arms, Bethlehem Steel and General Electric.
Pretty much the same situation has developed in this country, and we find the large corporations being given major orders and then developing their own institutions to the point where they can take care of much that is required in the way of component parts. I find similar complaints voiced by the mayor of the city of London who, on returning to his home city after visiting Ottawa, said:
"It was difficult to find out exactly how industry should go about getting contracts directly from the Department of Munitions and Supply," he said. "By persistence it developed that practically all the large prime contractors had been selected already and that only these were being asked to tender on new jobs. Therefore he' advised London industrialists to appeal directly to other manufacturers with prime contracts for war work."

We have a prime contract at the city of Regina, and the management of that plant for the time being must, because of conditions which it is not necessary to discuss, obtain their manufactured component parts from certain eastern connections. It is equally true that the management has been instructed by the Department of Munitions and Supply to obtain its manufactured component parts in western Canada, but in the search for these manufactured component parts they have spread their requirements from Winnipeg clear through to Vancouver. They have not attempted to centralize it in Saskatchewan but have distributed it pretty fairly over the three prairie provinces and to some extent in British Columbia. As far as our machine shops in Saskatchewan are concerned; as far as our other producers are concerned, all we ask is reciprocity, similar consideration. There is an office of the minister's department in the city of Winnipeg, and manufacturers have gone there seeking places where component parts could be manufactured; but because of the freight regulations in effect, because of freight tariffs that have burdened the development of western Canada for many years, they refuse to go further than Winnipeg. The Eastern Car company is an example. They refused to consider employment of any subcontractor for the manufacture of component parts west of Winnipeg, and the only reason given is freight rates. The Ogden shops at Calgary have substantial orders, but these shops, although they were instructed so to do, to my knowledge, have to a very limited extent distributed the manufacture of component parts. Western Steel Products, another company that has been favoured with large war contracts, has not utilized its own facilities either in Regina or in Saskatoon for the manufacture of component parts or anything else. My only thought is that the minister's Winnipeg office should be clothed with some authority in the distribution of war orders and in the spreading out of contracts for the manufacture of component parts.

Mr. Chairman, I had almost completed what I wished to say. In conclusion, I would point out to the minister that in Saskatchewan ours is a badly balanced economy, and that we are now reaping the harvest of that economy. We have regarded ourselves as an agricultural province and have tried to do that which we were best equipped to do, leaving the industrial production to other parts of Canada. A distribution system has been established in my province, but daily the components parts of that system are receiving notice from the eastern manufacturers that no longer will it be possible for them to deliver goods, that the goods produced in their plants are required in the immediate district in which they are produced. In other words, the central provinces are looking after their own customers. We have relied upon the eastern manufacturer, but he has not made an equitable distribution of the goods he has been able to produce in these strenuous times. He is depriving his western customer of those goods in order to supply local demands.
That is one reason why we are alarmed at the continued industrial expansion of eastern Canada. In the east we are building up an industrial Frankenstein which, immediately the war is over, will absorb our markets and keep us in the position we have occupied thus far, namely, hewers of wood and drawers of water for those who live in the more favoured parts of this country. We think that because of our contributions of men to the army, the navy and the air force, western Canada deserves a better deal by way of industrial expansion. We think it deserves greater consideration by the Department of National Defence in the matter of camps for the training of men. I was greatly interested in a question placed on the order paper by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), a question which I was afraid to ask. The hon. member wants to know the number of men who were recruited in Saskatchewan and the number of men who were trained in that province. I know that when that question is answered he will be told of the 500 men from Saskatchewan who have been sent to Lansdowne park, Ottawa, this year; of the 250 men who have been sent to Windsor; of the group sent
to Three Rivers; of another group sent to Sherbrooke; of another group from Dundum camp sent out to Chilliwack, British Columbia ; of the 450 men sent to Sarcee camp, notwithstanding the fact that we have a modem, well-equipped, up-to-date training camp at -Dumdum, Saskatchewan, which the Minister of National Defence has described as a "natural". At the present time we have fewer than two thousand men at that camp, and there have not been more than that there at any time.
I need not detain the committee any longer, Mr. Chairman, but I do ask for a better and fairer deal for the prairie provinces and in particular for the province of Saskatchewan, a deal that will enable us to assist in the solution of post-war problems.

Mr. Chairman, during the time this matter has been under discussion I have had a number of questions to ask, but either the minister has given the information himself, or other hon. members have asked the questions I had in mind, and I have avoided any repetition because I believe the valuable time of the minister should be used as effectively as possible. But under this bill we are spending tremendous sums of money, and my only reason for taking part in this debate is to say a word on behalf of the people whom I represent and who are helping to provide this money. The only thing we wish is to get full value for the money spent, and to be sure that in the spending of this money the munitions of war are made as quickly as possible, and in the largest possible quantities. The Department of Munitions and Supply and the Department of Labour are very closely connected, and in the spending of this money I want to impress upon the minister one matter which perhaps has not as yet been stressed sufficiently in this house; that is, that in the placing of contracts and the obtaining of supplies, it is not only a question of getting raw materials, having the machinery and the factories, and all the rest of it. There is also the human element, which plays such a tremendous part in production.
The question of morale has been mentioned in connection with the aircraft industry. I noticed that this afternoon the minister said he was satisfied that morale had reached a healthy stage; I believe those were his words. Personally I am continually surprised that morale is as good as it is among the working people of this country, considering the conditions under which many of them have to work. I really was surprised when I heard the minister say that he thought morale in the aircraft factories had reached a healthy stage. I wondered whether it was Mr. Bell who had given him that impression, because my infor-

mation, coming from the men who work in the aircraft factories, is to the effect that Mr. Bell is not doing a great deal to increase morale, that in fact, in their opinion, he has done something calculated to destroy it. Only the other day I received a letter from the international association of machinists, Montreal aircraft lodge No. 712, in which they discuss the question of morale among the workers. They say they think it is very timely that Mr. Bell has given attention to the problem of morale building, but they feel he has chosen a most unfortunate wTay of going about it. They say:
We are convinced that morale can never be built by the superficial method of having someone who is a virtual stranger to the workers in the industry touring the country and setting up citizens' committees. This particular lodge, No. 712, say that they can be very justly proud of the work they have done, together with the management and Mr. Bell, in raising the morale in the Montreal plants. They go on to cite many instances of the type of activity to which they have contributed. Then they say this:
We wish to emphasize that for appeals of this kind to win the greatest lesponse from the workers they must come from the ranks of the workers themselves, from their own chosen leaders in whom they place their confidence and trust.
I suggest that the minister might see to the proposals of the workers themselves, as well as to those of men like Mr. Bell, because from the men who day by day work in the factories a considerable influence may be brought to bear to increase production. They say:
Our proposals would be that an authoritative representative of labour, preferably a member or the international association of machinists, be appointed by the government to assist Mr. Bell.
We would propose further that an apparatus similar to the war production board in the United States be set up in Canada, and that the establishment of joint production committees be encouraged in every war plant in the country.
While we are discussing the question of morale we must point out that the speech which Mr. Bell recently made to the war labour organization production conference here on May 7, which was published in the press, has had a yTery bad effect on the morale of all war workers m this area.
We have refrained from replying to some of the allegations made in Mr. Bell's speech which are most bitterly resented by workers, because of our unwillingness to do anything which would endanger the spirit of national unity which we have striven to create. But we feel it is in order to point out here that speeches and

statements of this kind must inevitably have the effect of breaking down whatever good might develop out of Mr. Bell's desire to conduct a morale-building" campaign.
In the speech to which they refer, Mr. Bell is reported to have said that the workers in industry were "in the front line-like hell." In my opinion a statement of that kind was an insult to the workers of this country, and certainly it would not be one -Hdiich would help to build up their morale.
I know, myself, that morale is an intangible thing. Yet it is built up upon certain concrete and physical things. But no man going around to industry and giving pep talks to the men is going to increase morale. However, unless we do have an increase in morale in this country we are never going to have the total war effort which we are supposed to be having, and which we have pledged to the other countries fighting in this war-the allies.
We must have a total war effort. We cannot have it without better morale than we have at the present time. What does morale depend upon? I am not just speaking of aircraft factories; I am speaking of factories in general. It seems to me that morale is built up on certain things. The main factor would, in my opinion, be this: the physical and mental health of the working people, an understanding of what they are fighting for, and an assurance by the government that in this war effort it is a case of one for all and all for one, that one being Canada.
I remember at this time last year during the debate on the war appropriation bill I placed on record some figures with regard to loss of time in the United States due to strikes, sickness and industri?' accidents. Figures of that kind are rather difficult to get in Canada. In fact I have not been able to get anything very recent from the dominion bureau of statistics. But I did notice a while ago a report issued by the Canadian institute of public opinion, and a release by the Gallup poll. I know a Gallup poll is a Gallup poll, and that it is not anything like as authentic or as true as a statement from the dominion bureau of statistics. On the other hand it paints a fairly accurate picture in a very general way of conditions as they are.
The report of the Gallup poll published in the Toronto Daily Star states:
It has been estimated that there are some four million Canadian workers to-day, including farmers. Assuming a 48-hour week, and a 4-week month indications are that among employed people alone, 26,000,000 man-hours were lost through sickness in February, or

three and a quarter million man-days. A man-day, of course, represents the amount of worn done by one man in one day.
To put the same thing in another way, this means that every Canadian worker on the average, lost six and a half hours, or four-fifths of an entire working day, because ot illness of some kind.
Here again I should like to be fair and say that in February sickness is possibly at its highest level, because there is more illness in winter, mostly by way of colds. The report of the Gallup poll goes on to say:
In terms of production, this amount of lost time equals approximately 370 medium bombers, or 70 corvettes, or 377 cruiser tanks.
I know these are very general figures; they are not specific. But they do show what a saboteur of our total war effort sickness can be. When we consider the money we are spending to buy raw materials and the money we are putting into contracts, and then realize that at the same time we are permitting sickness, the thief of time, to destroy our total effort, it seems such an idiotic thing that we have not done something to combat it, to get more for our money, more for our people, and speed up production by keeping the people in a state of physical health whereby they may contribute as they want to do.
I can quite agree that sickness is one of the arch saboteurs of Canada's war effort. As long as we have sickness going on as it is to-day, without something more being done to ensure health to our working people, a great deal of the money being spent on war appropriations is not going to be used as expeditiously as it should be. Nor is it going to give us the value it should, because at the present time the whole value in munitions of war is to get the war won quickly, and not to continue it unduly into the future.

I know, of course, that on March 2, 1942, order in council P.C. 1550 was passed. To tell the truth, I did not know anything about this order in council until I saw it mentioned in the Toronto Star. I do not know whether hon. members are able to keep pace with these orders in council, but I confess that I cannot. In my opinion it certainly would have been a good thing if this matter had been discussed before the order in council was passed. As far as orders in council go, if they can be considered as being good, this is one of the best. However, I do not believe for one moment that sufficient attention is being paid to the care of our working people. It is by such things that morale can be built up. In the same article which appeared in the Toronto Star on April 13, 1942, mention was made of this Gallup poll. It says:
Doctor J. J. Heagerty, chief of the dominion public health service, has written that tuberculosis rates are beginning to rise in Canada. The reason for it, he says, are the longer hours, the intense strain, the inadequate diets and the low standard of living still prevalent among many workers.
