The basic question affecting the health of our people is not the sanitary arrangements in the factories in which they work; it is the amount of wages they need to give them necessary food which is a primary consideration in building up the health of a people. We should realize the amount of time lost in this country through strikes and other causes. Because of strikes in 1941 there were 23,997 days lost. In a whole year only 23,997 days were lost because of strikes, but according to the Gallup poll, in the month of February alone 3,125,000 man days were lost from sickness. Some people think that our industrial workers have sabotaged the war effort with strikes; but when we come to analyse the reason for strikes, we find that it is, first, wage disputes and, second, the question of collective bargaining. In most instances the attempt to obtain collective bargaining by the workers is made so that they may be in a position to bargain for better wages rather than go on strike. If more money were expended to build up the health and morale of our people, we would not be losing 3,215,000 man days in a month like February.
In my opinion the Minister of Munitions and Supply has more to do than just to consider where various contracts should be placed. As a minister of this government it is part of his responsibility to see that the workers in our factories are given an opportunity to make their maximum contribution. It is part of his responsibility to use properly the money which he is expending through these contracts in order to get the most value and to produce things more speedily. I believe the minister has said already that the contracts have always been turned out in time, that all that Great Britain and Russia have been asking for has been supplied by the factories. But if we had not lost time through sickness and industrial accidents, these contracts could have been filled much sooner than they were and we could have gone on with other contracts. Our war effort could have been speeded up just that much more.
Perhaps the Minister of Munitions and Supply considers that these things are outside his department, but in my opinion he shares responsibility with the Minister of Labour and with others of the government to see that we do not lose time through strikes, sickness and other causes. Because of that I would urge upon him that if he wants to build up the morale of the people of this country, he should not listen to men like Mr. Bell. Rather he should listen to the legitimate demands of the workers in the industrial plants who are working and have been working for a long 
time in order to obtain the right guaranteed by this house of parliament, the right of collective bargaining. If it were mandatory tj give that right to the workers in industry, I dare to say that we could speed up the war effort considerably and provide more munitions and other things in which the minister is interested.
The second requisite for building up morale is to look after the mental health of our people. The industrial workers want to know why they are asked to speed up, why they are asked to accept certain hours of labour and so on. Not only that, they want to be assured that in this war it is a case of one for all and all for one. I dare to say that at the present time the industrial workers are not satisfied that in this war it is a case of one for all and all for one. Ninety-nine per cent of the people of Canada are willing to sacrifice and are already sacrificing for the sake of this war. They are not afraid to go on sacrificing, to sacrifice even more than they are at the present time. But the 99 per cent of the people who are sacrificing are not satisfied in their minds that the other one per cent of the Canadian people are doing their share of sacrificing. In fact, in the minds of many people there is a great deal of apprehension that the one per cent, those who control industry in this country, are more concerned at the present time about what is going to happen to them after the war than they are with putting everything they have into the winning of this war and making the sacrifices which are demanded of them.
That is the thing which is causing an unhealthy mental condition among thousands and thousands of Canadian people. Do any of us know where we shall be after the war is over? Thousands and thousands will be underneath the sod with nothing but a little cross over them, if they are lucky enough to get that. Many will be blown to smithereens long before there is a chance of picking them up and putting them together in order to put them underneath the ground. After the war is over, many will be in the relief lines again. No; this one per cent, those who are to-day in charge of the industry of this country, must realize that they will be very lucky if they come through this war. They will be very lucky if we win this war. They must realize that if through their own selfishness, if because they refuse to go ahead maybe and increase their production, because they are afraid that after the war they will not be able to make their profits, if they refuse to make the sacrifices, if by any chance we lose the war they will find out that German big busi-

ness will kill them just as effectively as German bombs can kill women and children in the cities of Europe.
Let us consider the long history of the war against Hitler. I do not like to be too severe in my criticism, but through the long years of the war against Hitler the record of this present government has been a rotten one. It has been a record of appeasement, and the government know it. The individual members of this government have all along taken a position of isolationism and appeasement to Hitler. The people of this country want to see from this government no more appeasement. I think they are pretty well satisfied that the government do not now want to appease Hitler, but what they are afraid of is that the government are appeasing the one per cent. As long as they have that feeling in their minds it is going to be difficult to build morale and get a total war effort.
As far as the workers of Canada are concerned, I know they are out to win the war. They are going to win the war; they are going to defeat Hitler. But the thing I would like this government to consider is this. Are the people going to win this war with this government-or in spite of it? They are going to win it; of that they are sure, and I am sure; and if they do not come to feel that they can win it in cooperation with the government, it may be necessary that they change some of those who to-day are conducting our war effort. It will be necessary to find men who are not willing to appease, but rather men who are willing to listen to the voice of the working people and to build national unity and build morale so that we can attain to a total war effort.
Labour itself has said that it wants to be treated as a responsible group. Only the other day I received a copy of a speech which was made by Elliot M. Little, Director of National Selective Service, on May 9, when he spoke before the Canadian Weekly Newspapers Association, and I would commend heartily the sentiments he expressed in that speech. If we had more of that attitude expressed not only by men like Mr. Little but by our leading industrialists, we would have a far better tone of morale in this countiy. I should like to quote briefly what Mr. Little said:
Do not mistake what I am talking about. By better employer-employee relations I do not mean a concession to the workers here, a privilege there, such as a cup of tea at four o'clock. Those things have their place. I am talking about the whole broad field of personnel management which boils down to mean the best possible personal relations between management and the employees. The workers I meet and have worked with do not want employers to hold their hand. They simply asked to be treated as you want to be treated-as an adult and a responsible citizen.
Considering the times and the circumstances, considering what is being asked of our workers to-day, I think it is high time factory managers and employers recognized this and, having recognized it, do something about it.
Men do better work if they feel they are working with you and not merely for you. I know what amazing benefits will flow from away down the line, if men are encouraged to take an interest in their jobs and in the operation of the plant. I will go this far: I feel certain that if the masses of our workers were permitted that interest in their plant, and allowed a reasonable voice in the affairs of their plant, many of the problems now hampering our production efforts would disappear.
Labour itself has expressed its opinion and has said in relation to the filling of contracts that if only it could share with the management the right to suggest improvements, it is positive that it could speed up the work which has to be done.
I noticed in PM magazine of April 13 an article which deals specifically with this very question in the United States, and I see no reason why there should be a difference between the United States and Canada. The article says:
Colt's Patent Fire-arms Manufacturing Company, situated in an open-shop stronghold, is one of the first companies in New England to form a labour-management production cimmittee.
It also says that immediately after this committee was set up, the management wanted to see what help they could get from it, and so they asked the union to investigate why, during the early days of the contract, spoiled machine-gun barrels in one plant were running to 17 per cent. With company encouragement union shop stewards investigated. The article goes on to say:
This ordinarily would be a "management" problem.
But because the company had the cooperation of the union this is what happened:
Union shop stewards investigated. The stewards found the faults: defective steel, improper inspection, and the fact that some operators were wandering away from their automatic borers.
The union representatives reported their discoveries to the management and spoke quietly to the errant operators, with the result that spoilage was reduced to eight-tenths of 1 per cent. That was quite a reduction from 17 per cent.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has been good enough to give this committee some account of the war production of this country at the present time. He has told us something of the number of machine guns, tanks, automatic rifles, automotive equipment and many other individual items, that are being manufactured, I find myself, however, in the position of a builder who has a lot of materials but no general blueprint to which to work. I know that the minister will know and appreciate just what that feeling is, for without a plan it is difficult to know what to do with the materials which we may collect. All hon. members understand that, when a modem sky-scraper goes up-and after all we must liken the war effort to that-the steel framework goes up first, and the bricks and all the parts are merely fillers-in to finish the completed building. I do not think the minister, despite the pains he has taken at times to give us information, has yet given us the general framework of our industrial contribution to this war. I would1 ask him, there-

War Appropriation-Supplies
fore, what is the blueprint, what is the general plan? What are we aiming to accomplish from an industrial point of view? It is hardly enough to say that we are busy. We cannot proceed helter-skelter. We must proceed according to plan if things are to go along smoothly and we are to avoid bottlenecks and achieve the maximum production of which we are capable.
Let us take, for example, the steel supply in this country. What do hon. members know about the considerations which entered the minds of the government when steel was first considered in the early days of the war, or even after the fall of France, or even at the present time? How much has this country expanded its iron and steel production so that we shall have enough of that basic commodity out of which nearly all armaments are made?
May I ask the minister, for instance, what were the considerations which his department entertained when the Ojibway plant was considered, as I assume it must have been considered at some time? If I am correctly informed, some two years ago it was understood that this plant, which had never been brought into production as a steel producing unit, although parts of it had been been brought into production as a fabricator of steel products, would have required no less than two years and possibly twenty-five million dollars to bring it in as a great steel producer. What were the expectations in the mind of the government at that time, that they did not go ahead with the production of steel at the Ojibway plant, entailing, as I have said, two years of time and possibly twenty-five million dollars? When did the minister and the government expect the peak of industrial war production would occur in this country? Would it be in 1941, let us say the fall of that year, or in 1942, or in 1943?
These are major problems which hon. members should consider, and they should be given information, to some extent at least, in so far as the government can do so without giving away secrets which would be valuable to the enemy, so that we may know what we are aiming to accomplish, what we can reasonably expect to do; and we, not a few closeted together, should have something to say and should be able to make some contribution to the decisions which are made.
May I ask him also whether or not I am correctly informed that the Canadian Car and Foundry company had a steel-producing plant at Welland, Ontario, a plant which made a fairly notable contribution during the last war to war production, and yet has only recently been dismantled, during this war, not having turned a wheel?
I saw in the Montreal Gazette not long ago a dispatch from the New York Times of February 16, stating that Japan's scrap steel supply was ten million tons, all from the United States, and that it was held that this would be enough to last for three years. With Japan four thousand and more miles away from this continent, why was it that we in Canada did not make available to ourselves some of the scrap which went to that country? It is a fact that we are not producers of iron ore in any quantity ourselves. The situation is somewhat different from the production and export of some of our own minerals, because we have them in the bowels of the earth to-day and can get them out for our own production, perhaps not so fast as we should like; nevertheless we have them. But we have not a commodity like scrap, and at the present time we cannot get it in sufficient quantity to achieve the maximum production which I am sure the minister himself would like to see.
In fact the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) last night stated that some of the scrap which Japan got came from Canada, and I noticed that his statement was not challenged. Were we afraid at that time, as a country, to borrow from the United States in order to accumulate this very necessary supply of scrap for armament purposes in this country? We all knew that we were faced with the possibility of war, and that we must import iron ore and scrap if we were to engage in a major struggle. It is true that we have some of these materials ourselves, but not nearly enough to carry on a major conflict. Or was it that Canada was unwilling to put restrictions on the consumption of goods imported from the United States so that we could accumulate sufficient United States dollars with which to purchase scrap and store it in this country?
Only last summer a delegation from Toronto waited upon the steel controller in order to obtain a priority for the construction of a sewage disposal plant in that city. The director, who was then new to his office, explained to us that he believed that our cause was a very necessary one, and that, inasmuch as we would need the steel, not immediately but in a few months-the first requirement would then be needed and it would extend perhaps over two years-it would not be unlikely that we could get the steel. However, he had been in his office only a few weeks, and, shall I say, had not become politically conscious, as every civil servant must be to some extent, and he said, "So far we have no balance sheet." That is, after two years of war the Minister of Munitions and Supply did not have-if I take this state-
War Appropriation-Supplies

ment at its full worth, and I see no reason why I should not-a balance sheet of the steel production and the steel requirements of this countiy. He did not know in what form he could get iron and steel, what shapes were available, what the needs of essential civilian industry would be, and what would be available for war industry.
If I am mistaken in the presentation of this picture I know the minister will correct me. But I also took some steps to check the impression which I gained, and I found, from what I could learn, it was by no means an incorrect one. Is it any wonder then, Mr. Chairman, we find that there is an announcement on the part of the government that two destroyers will be built, and then, that this programme is to be cancelled because the steel is not available in this country and cannot be purchased in the United States?
These are things which parliament and the people of Canada want to know.
There are many small, vexatious and perhaps inconsequential things, like delays when there is a change-over from production of one model to another. But it is the vast general plan, respecting steel, aluminum and other essential products which are what one might call primary products and which go into the making of the finished article, with which we are deeply concerned.
There have been times when the shipyards have been closed down temporarily because of shortage of steel in particular forms. Why is it that, when we have steel in great quantities available for some things, we do not have it available for other things? Of course, the answer is that certain implements of war have priority. But the questions which this committee should be informed about, so that they may have a reasonable opinion on them, are questions like these.
There is a plant not very far from where I live which is turning out millions of large shells every year-a tremendous and extremely creditable output. The amount of steel which is consumed in the production of these shells must be staggering. Yet we find there is a shortage of steel for certain other commodities. Would the minister explain to the committee, if it is not a military secret, just what is being done with these shells? Is too much steel going into that production as against certain other essential war materials which require steel? We should have some understanding as to why so many shells continue to be turned out even though this has not yet developed into what we would call a shooting war.
Again, we are now to produce aero engines. That subject came up in the house a year or

eighteen months ago and it was held that it was not worth while, that it was not economically feasible to use certain of our productive capacity and our mechanics for the making of aircraft engines. Yet we find that only within the last few months, within recent times at any rate, we have begun a programme of building a fairly simple aero engine. Surely mechanics are scarcer to-day than they were when the subject was first mooted in this house.
I should like the minister to say a word or two about his experience with industrial councils. They are now coming to the fore more and more, and I notice that his director-general of aircraft production stated that he had found them very useful. It may be that the workers in industry have something to contribute in the way of ideas to management. We hear a great deal about this nowadays, and I feel that the minister must have had many reports sent him as to what can be accomplished in the way of workers sharing by contributing their ideas to .more effective management. One cannot help feeling, on the other hand, that the problems of management are very grave. Managers are for the most part qualified men who have had experience; nevertheless, most of the managers in this country and in the United States are, like Mr. Knudsen, men who have themselves come up from the ranks of industry, and it is the same type of brains they have that exists in the ranks, only perhaps in a lesser degree.
I have been informed also that there are certain difficulties in some of the departments -and I do not think the Department of Munitions and Supply is any exception in this regard-in finding capable men to carry out the war effort. It is difficult to get men through the civil service because of the regulations and the fixed salaries there. Perhaps the minister would outline the situation to us. There are civil servants who have been given very much greater responsibilities because of war work, and I am told that there are civil servants to-day who are getting $1,500 to $2,000 though they have assistants from outside business who are second or third in command, and who receive substantially more than themselves. Surely the rules of the civil service are not so rigid, so impossible to rectify, that recognition cannot be given the splendid work which some civil servants are doing and the responsibilities which they now bear, responsibilities which are out of proportion to those which they had prior to the war.
Before leaving the subject to which I referred this afternoon, namely the Hirst matter, I do not want the minister to feel that those of us on this side of the house do not recognize

War Appropriation-Supplies
what a serious principle is involved in what I may term dereliction on the part of the director-general of aircraft production. We know that he is a splendid man in many ways. We understand that he is doing a good job, and there is no desire to hamper in any way the maximum production of aircraft. But I am constrained to point out to the minister that if he allows directors of production, or directors anywhere throughout the government sendee, to commit these faults, very serious faults, such as the one in question, and says that we cannot do anything about it; that we have two alternatives-either to dismiss the man or to retain him; if we adhere to the policy which I hope is the right one in this case, namely, that of retaining the man; nevertheless, we are putting these dollar-a-year men, some of them directors of production, in a position where they become a power above parliament. We must have men who will act according to the principles which must obtain in the carrying on of government business. We cannot have men given the tremendous power which a director of production has to-day and have such men abuse that power by taking away business from citizens of the country and giving it to those whom they favour. It is a principle which is reprehensible and one which the minister has admitted to be such. What I want to point out is the general principle behind the retention of a man who does such things. While willing to make an exception in this case, I want the minister to know that we feel deeply that an essential principle is at stake in this matter.
I cannot help saying a word here about the letter of endorsation which the minister brought down in the house last Friday, whereby various members of the aircraft industry-endorsed this morale building campaign undertaken by Mr. Bell through Mr. Hirst. It would have been better if the minister had left that alone. Here he is in a position of awarding contracts to every one of these aircraft producers. Their action may have been spontaneous; I do not know to the contrary ; but they produce a letter signed by each one of them endorsing what is admitted by all in this house to have been an act which should not be too lightly condoned. Perhaps I should not say they put their stamp of approval on it, but they certainly put their stamp of approval on the subject matter around which the whole thing revolved, namely, the morale-building campaign.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: May I interrupt to ask if the hon. gentleman is suggesting that the resolution from the industry was not spontaneous? I want him to answer yes or no.

I do not think I am required to answer the question. I did not say it was not spontaneous, but let me tell the minister this. That letter was signed, I suppose, by every aircraft manufacturing company in this country; but what amazed me mostly was to see the name of Trans-Canada Air Lines, a wholly owned government corporation, supervised by the minister himself, on it. The minister might just as well have signed it.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: My hon. friend can accept this or not. It just so happened that while this debate was on, the gentlemen represented by those signatures were in conference in Ottawa, and they walked into my office at a quarter to three on the day I presented the letter and asked me to accept it. I thought it of interest to the committee and I read it. If the hon. gentleman suggests that there was propaganda on my part, or on the part of any officer of my department, I wish he would withdraw the suggestion or accept the onus of the statement, because this should be publicized.
I do not feel myself compelled to do either. If the minister thinks I suggested that he did it, he may read that into my remarks. I did not intend that he should.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: What was the purpose of saying it?

I think the speaker is required by the rules to accept a statement made by some hon. member whom he is criticizing with regard to that gentleman's own actions. I think the hon. gentleman should accept the minister's statements in that regard.
I accept the statement of the minister that it was spontaneous on the part of the aircraft producers. I am not surprised that it should be because they are all beholden to him for contracts.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: That is my hon. friend's opinion. Take a look at him, imputing motives.

Not at all. I want to point out this, that the power which the minister has to-day is perhaps the greatest power in this country. He has, according to his own statement, placed contracts to the value of four billion dollars, a sum which he states was greater than the total debt of this country prior to the war. Every citizen of this Canada of ours knows the power that is his through the spending of the $15 or $20 a week he may earn, at the comer grocery store or the chain store, and these stores all compete for his money. In the same way industry competes for the orders given out by the

War Appropriation-Supplies

minister; it is anxious to get those orders, and there is not a single industry of any size in this country that cares to run foul of the Minister of Munitions and Supply.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I think the industry would
be very glad to know my hon. friend's view of their action. I think they will be glad to know that they are accused of kowtowing to my power and trying to please me. I had nothing to do with that letter. I stated that I took no responsibility for it, that I believed it was a very improper letter. The industry had no particular reason to please me, but I shall be glad to have the public know the view my hon. friend takes of their action.

I must say I do not feel very badly about what the minister has just said. Some of my friends are in the industry, and personally I would think the minister was not well advised in bringing the letter down here.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: A very cheap remark!

The minister is very fond of saying things about various people. I might mention a few things he said during one day, Mr. Chairman. He referred to one hon. member's speech as "hysterical" and to the hon. member as a displayer of "histrionics." We in this house are great sinners if we dare to rise in our places and criticize the Department of Munitions and Supply. Another hon. member was called a perpetrator of "trick questions"; another was admonished not to talk so "glibly"; another was told he was making a "sales talk," while still another was advised to "stick to matters that he could understand." All I can say is that when I find myself in such good company I really do not feel badly off at all.
The minister has said that the opposition, and even some members of his own party who occasionally have matters they wish to bring up, should not rely on gossip. I should like to tell him one reason why we have to rely on information which may not be quite as authentic as scripture. I find that business men who favour the principles of the party of which I am a member but who, like all business men to-day, are doing business with the government in one way or another, do not want to be seen with Conservative members because they are afraid it might work to their disadvantage.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I think there may be other
reasons.
I am not suggesting that the minister has any gestapo or anything like that to watch over them, but they do not like to be seen-

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Do not be too sure of the
reason, though.

Thank you very much;
that is another of the innuendoes which the minister is so fond of handing out. However, it is a fact that it is most difficult to get information because, as we know, this is a party government; there is no national government, as so many of us on this side would prefer to see. We are not interested in politics, and I hope I am not talking politics now.
Oh, oh.

I want to read to this
committee a document for which the minister is responsible, which I think is one of the principal reasons for our failure to get authentic information. Let me read the oath which is required to be taken by every officer of the Department of Munitions and Supply, and this oath applies to men who are appointed as directors of government corporations and who are serving without remuneration.

Including a number of
Conservatives.

Indeed, yes; in fact it
was a Conservative who let me know about this. I dare say the minister would like to call out, "Who is he"? so that I might name somebody, and then possibly the services of that gentleman, at SI a year, would be terminated. This oath applies to our friends the dollar-a-year men who might furnish us with responsible information. My good friends to the left do get information from their particular sources. They get some of it from working men, as we do, and in addition some of us happen to know these dollar-a-year men. Here is the oath:
I . . . solemnly swear that I will faithfully and honestly fulfil the duties which devolve upon me and shall not divulge any knowledge or information obtained by me in the course of my employment to anyone not employed by the Department of Munitions and Supply unless expressly authorized by my superior officers. So help me God.
What is wrong with that oath?
If you wish us to make constructive suggestions, surely members of parliament can be trusted with the information these men may have; and if the minister does not want us to rely on gossip-
Is that oath not similar to the civil service oath?

Order.

War Appropriation-Supplies

If the minister is not opposed to our obtaining correct information; if he does not wish us to have to rely on what he terms "gossip", surely he would be willing to put through an amendment to that oath, to make it read, "shall not divulge any knowledge or information obtained by me in the course of my employment to anyone, other than members of parliament, not employed by the Department of Munitions and Supply". That would be purely permissive; it would not make them tell anything they did not want to tell. But as ordinary business men, surely these men can be trusted. Those appointed as dollar-a-year men are placed in those positions, by the minister if you like, because they are men who are able to hold their tongues when they should, and who do not talk out of turn. But surely if they believe that something is wrong and that it should.be rectified in parliament, they should be in a position to tell their member about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I would not speak again but for the fact that my hon. friend has made two statements which I should correct. In the first place he said we have given up the idea of building destroyers because we *cannot get steel. I do not think it is any secret that the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services attended the ceremony of the laying of the keels of two destroyers some days ago. The other statement was that we are building aeroplane engines in Canada. That is not correct. I have stated many times in this house that we believe our industrial effort can be used to better advantage than in the building of aeroplane engines; that we had made satisfactory arrangements for all the aeroplane engines we required for our programme, and that we did not intend to manufacture aeroplane engines in this country.
Then the hon. gentleman wished a blueprint of Canada's war effort. If he could give me an accurate blueprint of the progress of Canada's war for this year, next year or any other time, I think I could give him an accurate blueprint of Canada's industrial effort for a concurrent period. But I think all we can do is try reasonably to anticipate the requirements of the war and plan our course from week to week and month to month accordingly. We have had an objective, which is to put into the hands of Canadian troops every weapon and every supply they require to carry on the war and to make them the best equipped troops in the world. Beyond that it has been our 44561-168}
objective to make the maximum contribution to the munitions programme of the allied armies as a whole. We have found that certain lines of production are particularly adapted to this country, and we have gone full out on those lines. Certain exigencies of the war have made it necessary for us to go full out in directions which we did not intend to go in earlier stages. We have changed our course from time to time, as the developments of the war have indicated. We have watched our material situation very carefully. We have had a well-considered chart of that from the beginning, and had that not been so we would have had no mtmitions programme to-day. I say that because we have expanded our programme beyond anything that could have been anticipated eighteen months ago.
In the matter 6f steel Canada has never been self-contained. It has been our custom to import from the United States about a third of our steel requirements. We determined to plan our programme on continued importations in the same proportions. We discussed the matter thoroughly with responsible officers in the United States, and it was agreed that if we maintained this proportion we could reasonably count on the United States furnishing the same proportion of our requirements that had been their custom to furnish in peace time.
We have increased our production. Our billets production to-day is about 50 per cent greater than pre-war capacity. To those who know the time and money involved in developing capacity for basic steel, the tremendous increase will be readily understood. No other country in the world has, I think, had the same proportionate increase in the same period. I am speaking of basic steel.
In the matter of alloy steel we have gone considerably farther, and we have multipled our pre-war capacity by more than five, and, I think, more than six times, to make possible the gun programme and other programmes involving the use of alloy steel in this country.
My hon. friend has said that we have no balance sheet. The interview he had took place at a time when we were moving from a system of priorities into a system of definite allocation. The practice is to-day to place in the hands of every producer of steel1 a rolling schedule which will cover his rollings for the next month, and to attach to that schedule definite allocations for every pound of steel that is rolled. That requires, as hon. members know, an accurate balance sheet. It requires an accurate forecast of steel requirements for the succeeding months, and an accurate breakdown into rolling schedules.
War Appropriation-Supplies

In the first phase of the war steel was not as tight. We could get along very well with priorities; that is, giving the first call on steel to types of production where war requirements were most urgent. We have watched our raw materials situation very closely. However, we have not proceeded timidly; rather we have proceeded boldly. We have stretched our resources, as we think, to their limit. Under these circumstances it is not surprising that the increase in raw products sometimes gets out of step with the increase in finished goods. There are times when finished goods are planned at a certain rate of production, and it is found that the machines will do better than anticipated, and turn out an increased production. Unfortunately we cannot stretch basic steel production as we can the production of finished goods, and we have situations where we have temporary [DOT] shortages of steel. Similarly, in connection with United States steel, on which we depend, and which is about a third of our total supply, we have found difficulties from time to time. Our shipments get out of step, and we do have shortages. Such conditions are inevitable, if we want to proceed boldly and get the last ounce of finished production out of our factories. But the situation is improving all the time. Production is coming in from the factories, and these delays are getting less as time goes on. We hope they will shortly be eliminated. We still have considerable basic steel production coming in. I think we have a half million ton capacity of pig-iron under construction at the present time. Part of that will be in in July of this year, and part of it in the early months of next year.
We have carefully assessed our scrap capacity, and the ability of this country to produce scrap. We believe that that situation is well in hand. My hon. friend rather implied that while the Japanese had been piling up the scrap we had done nothing about it. As a matter of fact we have in this country substantial reserves of scrap which we are doing everything possible to protect, through salvage campaigns.
My hon. friend asks why we did not proceed with steel development at Ojibway. The situation at Ojibway is this:	Two blast
furnaces were built there many years ago. They were never brought into production. Essential parts of the furnaces, such as blowing equipment, which is in fact the most important part of a furnace, were never supplied. The only operation carried on there was galvanizing of steel plate. That, of course, is not in any way an operation having to do with basic steel. The furnaces were there; we looked at them at the earliest

opportunity to see whether they would offer a reasonable point at which to expand our steel production. It is quite obvious from the report made to me by the best experts in this country that the same capacity could be obtained very much more cheaply by expanding the steel plants already in operation. The expansion at Ojibway meant putting in coal-handling equipment, ore-handling equipment and dock facilities. The docks there are not in any way equipped. It involved improving the blast furnaces which, while modern at the time they were installed, are entirely out of date to-day. They are not of the size or capacity which anyone would buy or install at this time. As I say, the expense was vastly greater than would be the expense of expanding the existing plants. The result is that our expansion was made at existing plants, namely Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation at Sydney, the Steel Company of Canada at Hamilton, Canada Foundries and Forgings Limited at Hamilton, and the Mgoma Steel Company at Sault Ste. Marie. We have stepped these plants up, and balanced them up, until we have increased our production of basic steel by more than 50 per cent over the pre-war capacity.
We have expanded our production of aluminum in this country by some five times. We have heard a great deal about the expansion of aluminum production in the United States, but to-day in Canada we have a greater capacity for aluminum production than we ever had in our history. I think about 44 per cent of the aluminum which is produced on this continent is produced in this country.
We have carefully weighed our power resources, and have stepped them up in a practical way. Our industries have been distributed to use those resources to the utmost. I believe to-day we are making a very efficient use of the power at our disposal.
The hon. member mentioned one further point, namely the oath of secrecy. We thought we should go the whole way, because we were doing very secret work with secret weapons. For clients in connection with whom secrecy was necessary we thought we should go the whole way. We made provision that our employees must obtain the consent of their senior officers before information could be given to anyone. I think that is the usual form, and I think there are few countries in the world that do not exact that oath from employees handling confidential war documents.

TFar Appropriation-Supplies

I presume the minister has no objection to members of parliament who represent the people of Canada having the information at their disposal. That would not force his dollar-a-year men to give information; it simply puts them in a position where they would feel that they are not breaking their oath.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: My hon. friend has been a member of parliament for a sufficient length of time to know there is a proper way to obtain any information that he wishes from any department of government. The proper way is to apply to the minister of the department for the information. As he knows, it is highly improper for a member of parliament to go to a deputy minister or a minor officer in the department fo obtain information, particularly information which he intends to use in this house. The net result of that is that he embarrasses a man who has no protection except the ordinary protection he gets in his duties. I think it is highly improper for any member of parliament to question an officer of a department for material which he intends to use in this house. I think the position in the Department of Munitions and Supply is exactly the same as that in any other department of government. I have men delegated for the express purpose of providing information to members of parliament when that information is asked for through myself. I challenge any hon. member to say that he has been denied any information by my office when he applied for it in the ordinary way.

I have greatly enjoyed the discussion thus far, but I believe we should revert for a time to the question of labour supply and the attitude of labour. That there is a most gratifying extension of Canada's war production, no one could possibly doubt. One great danger I see, however, is the spread of deterioration in the morale of our labouring ranks. I have seen some evidence of great indiscretion during the last two or three months with respect to labouring men. I should like to comment on the labour situation and draw to the minister's attention some of the causes for anxiety that I feel exist.
As an example of the sort of thing that I think ought not to appear in Canada, may I refer to a leaflet which came to my desk not a great while ago. This contained advanced pages from the May, 1942, issue of Industrial Canada. The heading of the leaflet is "Recent appeals by the press in the United States and Canada for an all-out war effort." I read this through with some care and marked certain passages which I rather wished had not
appeared in print in Canada. One of these appeared in the Windsor Star of April 21, 1942, and it reads:
The workers in our shipyards are undoubtedly entitled to fair and decent treatment. They are entitled to take every fair and decent means to obtain it. They are not entitled to demand the lives of soldiers and sailors in order to gain their ends.
I think we must all grant that there can be no objection to what the words say, but what the words imply is extremely offensive. There may be nothing wrong with this, but what came into my mind was: What is a fair wage? I wonder if it ever entered the minds of the printers of the Windsor Star to canvass the whole wage situation in Canada in order to determine what would be a fair wage and then examine the wages paid in the particular plants involved to see whether they conformed to the level of desirable wages throughout Canada? There is in evidence the greatest amount of loose, slipshod, careless and unscientific thinking on this matter. The former Minister of Labour (Mr. McLarty) is looking at me very earnestly, but I think he will agree with me that there is a lack of objectivity in thinking with respect to the wage situation in this country.
The only thing is that I doubt if it is the duty of one particular newspaper to make an analytical study of all the wages paid in Canada to see if they are relatively fair and decent.

I will grant that it probably is not the duty of any particular newspaper; but when the newspaper endeavours to obtrude itself into a discussion and makes remarks which might be offensive to people, it pretty nearly becomes essential for that newspaper to have something constructive to offer.

I would not agree with the hon. member for Lethbridge. Newspapers do inject themselves into many discussions without assuming the basic responsibility of conducting a national canvass to see whether or not their observations are entirely well founded.

I did not rise to discuss newspapers, so I am not going any farther. I have said what I think and the minister has said what he thinks, so we will leave it at that. They say that labouring men are entitled to fair and decent treatment, but again there is a lack of objectivity. People are not agreed as to what constitutes fair and decent treatment, and the result is that bitterness is likely to be engendered. We must not have bitterness engendered in the minds of the men
War Appropriation-Supplies

or in the minds of their employers. The newspaper goes on to say that the men are entitled to take every fair and decent means. What are fair and decent means? To what can the miners or the labouring men resort?
The Industrial Disputes Act of this country stands out in bold relief when compared with any other form of labour legislation of a like nature.
Is it working to-day?
My hon. friend knows that it is working to-day.

The retort which naturally comes into one's mind is, "ye shall know them by their fruits." I believe before I get through I shall be able to show that there are sufficient fruits from the labour policy of this country to show that it is not working as it should.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Would my hon. friend let me interject a remark? The Minister of Labour and I made a very important engagement for 9.30 o'clock and we have been postponing it, relying on the fact that we would be kept here for only half an hour this afternoon. Would my hon. friend excuse us for a few moments and let the acting Minister of Labour carry on? I think it is going to be a labour argument, and we promise to return as soon as we can.
I will say to my hon. friend that the matter he is discussing is one my colleague and I are going to discuss, and it will affect the welfare of thousands of working men in this country.

Then I certainly wish the Minister of Labour could be here. May I just say to him that I think he is doing the job in a way that is going to make for improvement, and I wish him well in the very difficult task ahead. I was referring to certain passages in certain newspapers. I turn now to the Toronto Globe and Mail of April 14, 1942, where these words appeared:
We have not read that these gallant seamen are quarrelling with their employers about overtime pay. There can be no excuse for a shut-down in any Canadian shipyard. Unfortunately, Canada has had more than one. Less than ten days ago a Quebec shipyard was closed down pending adjustment of complaints about wage schedules.
Again there is an insinuation and an implication which is offensive. I notice that this paper attaches the blame entirely to the poor working men and never a word of blame to the man who is employing the men. If there develops in a plant ill feeling as a result of which the men feel themselves
[Mr. Blackmore.l
obliged to take drastic measures, no blame is attached to the man who goaded them on and refused to listen to their plea. That is entirely as it ought not to be. The paper goes on to say:
Men producing guns, tanks, planes and ships ought not to be allowed to down tools in face of the enemy. They are entitled to fair wages.
Again we have fair wages mentioned with no definition as to what fair wages are. I believe we will grant that the men who are working in munitions plants ought not to down tools, but may I say once more that the men who are managing these plants ought not to put the working men in a position where they are obliged to lay down their tools.
I turn to the Montreal Gazette of April 22, 1942. These newspapers by the way are commenting on the strike which took place in the shipyards at Midland and the sympathetic walk-out that took place in the Kingston plant. The Montreal Gazette says:
Shipyard workers at Midland, Ontario, downed their tools last Wednesday mainly because a semi-skilled workman had been dismissed or transferred. It does not appear to have been a good enough reason for paralysing an essential industry.
Once more the blame is attached to the men, and not to the man who dismissed this worker. We are not given any details to show whether the dismissal of this worker was justified. The whole thing is left in such a way as to cast reflections on the men who are working in our munitions plants. That is decidedly not fair; in fact, it is decidedly pernicious. May I read another passage from the same editorial?
Labour interests can be safeguarded, and where legitimate will be safeguarded, without the necessity of strikes which interrupt war production and are gifts to the enemies of this country.
If only Canada would safeguard those rights! If only we had the evidence to prove that they had been safeguarded! If only we had evidence to show that provision woidd be made to safeguard these rights, things would be so different from what they are to-day in Canada. I wish to point out to the minister that this situation is, in my judgment, exceedingly grave. It is far easier to keep men feeling enthusiastic when they are not bitter than to get them back into the right frame of mind after their morale has been destroyed. '
I believe that all the members of the federal cabinet who have anything to do either directly or indirectly with labour policy in this country ought to get together in the most earnest manner and, having regard to

War Appropriation-Supplies
the way in which labour problems are taken care of elsewhere, draft a policy which will be most completely designed to make the labouring men in Canada happy, for unhappy men cannot produce as well as happy men. The cabinet should have in their minds in approaching this task this principle, that they will make the labouring men in Canada partners in Canada's war effort and not servants in Canada's war effort.
There may be those who will think I am probably overstressing this matter but, Mr. Chairman, I find on the streets as I talk with the ordinary man here and there an antagonism to the interests of the labouring man which undoubtedly has been engendered by such things as the newspaper comments to which I have referred already in this speech. Such antagonism undoubtedly offends the labouring men whenever they come into contact with it. The whole effect is altogether undesirable. So I say that every cabinet minister who has anything to do with the labour situation in Canada should devote himself most earnestly to the drafting of the finest labour policy that can be drafted for this country.
In that policy there are several important principles which should be incorporated, and the first one is the principle of the fair wage. A board of men in Canada should be set the task of determining what a fair wage policy in Canada is; whether or not, we will say, a wage of $120 a month which might perhaps be fair in one city is fair in another city, and whether sufficient allowance is made for the cost of living and other considerations, so that we can be sure that the wage rate throughout Cainada from coast to coast is fair and equitable.
There will be those who will answer me in this way: "Now, look, you simply cannot have the wage rate in Canada raised without causing inflation. The freezing of wage rates is a necessary precaution against inflation." Let me answer them thus. Inflation is a rise in price. When men were given additional reward for their labour, if the added pay were not registered in increased -costs or increased prices there would be no inflation. The only danger then would be in having extra purchasing power going out into the hands of the people, which might, by their using the goods which were available, tend towards inflation.
There will be no increase in the costs of the articles produced if the government subsidizes the wage rate in a given plant so that the government pays the additional increase. Such procedure would obviate the necessity of the plant adding anything to its costs and raising prices.
Who will pay the subsidy?
The government will pay the subsidy.
Who is the government?
The government must use credit, the credit of Canada, to do it.
Where are we going to get the cash?

I know my hon. friend does not understand that. I know he is quite earnest and sincere, but may I tell him that he is living in the middle of the twentieth century, in a time when orthodox methods of finance can no longer safely be used or relied upon. There are financial principles as a result of the application of which the government can use the credit of Canada to increase the wages of the men working in plants without causing an increase in the costs of the goods those men are producing, and without causing additional taxation or occasioning additional borrowing.
Or inflation?
No, it is not inflation. Remember that inflation is a rise in price. Does my hon. friend accept that as the definition of inflation?
No.
That is true. I know my hon. friend does not know that, but I am telling him.

I wonder whether the hon. gentleman has analysed the experience in the last war as to the rise in the cost of living, which exceeded much the rise in wages as this rise in the cost of living progressed.

Now, Mr. Chairman: before very long, in this whole general debate, the question of inflation will be discussed in great detail. I am thoroughly familiar with what happened in the last war. I know the causes of it, and I know the way in which it could have been remedied and prevented. But to obtrude a discussion in detail on the subject of inflation at this time would probably not be in order, as the minister will acknowledge.
Quite true.

So that, while the subject is exceedingly interesting, and there is no subject which I would rather discuss, if he will permit me we will not go into inflation now. In passing, however, I wish to say one other thing about the question of inflation. I have shown that if the government pays the additional increase of the wage-

I think I have dealt enough with the question of inflation to show that there is no reason why the government cannot step into a given plant and, by subsidizing the rate of wage which is paid in that plant, raise all wages in that plant to a level which will be equitable.
The second principle which should be involved in our labour policy is the right to organize. I have under my hand at least seven different memoranda prepared and submitted by the labouring men throughout Canada, and I have magazines and other periodicals here which have been published in Canada in which are articles by men who are leaders of thought with respect to labour. In every single one of these the request is made that the men be given the right and allowed to exercise the right of organization and collective bargaining. I do not believe, sir, you can content the labouring men of Canada unless you give them that right and guarantee it to them and allow them to use it-the right to organize and to bargain collectively.
Why should Canada be the only one of the British countries in which this right of collective bargaining is denied the men. Why should it be possible to grant it to the men in Britain and the United States-
Does the hon. member suggest that any act of this government or any other government of Canada refuses the right to organize to employees in industry?
Another straw-man!

At another time
probably I shall discuss this matter in the

presence of the minister, and I believe he will be astounded to learn how completely this government-the government which holds office right now-has destroyed in Canada the right of collective bargaining.
Let us be fair about this. There is no act of this government which has disputed or in any way challenged the right of men engaged in industrial enterprise to organize.

And to bargain
collectively?
And to bargain collectively, yes.
And if a company discovers an organizer in its ranks and fires him, what does the government do?
Under the criminal code, if anyone is discharged by reason of the fact that he belongs to a legitimate trade union, the company concerned is subject to prosecution.
How many prosecutions have taken place?

I could not answer that question offhand. There are some that I remember quite well. There was one in Vancouver and, I believe, one in Montreal. I do not remember the actual number. Naturally, I have not the facts beneath my hand now. But there is a definite introduction into the criminal code, made, if I remember correctly, in 1938, that no man can be discharged from employment by reason of being a member of a trade union. It was introduced by this government.

I must perforce accept the word of the minister, but I believe he will find some difficulty in explaining the passage which I have already read from the Montreal Gazette:
Shipyard workers at Midland, Ont., downed their tools last Wednesday mainly because a semi-skilled workman had been dismissed or transferred. It does not appear to have been a good enough reason for paralysing an essential industry.
The minister will have upon his shoulders the burden of explaining why the men would consider it necessary to strike if they had assurance that their interests would be protected. I think the mere fact that these men in Midland did strike was the very best possible evidence that they had lost confidence in the government's willingness or ability, or both, or courage, to protect them in their demands to organize and bargain collectively.

As I say, I must accept what the minister said, but I have plenty of evidence, which I just do not happen to have under my hand and organized so that I can deal with the subject to-night, to show that in this country to-day there remains hardly anything substantial of the right of collective bargaining. It has been emasculated. It has a form of reality, but denies the power thereof.
The third principle which must be embodied in the labour policy of this country is that labour shall be permitted, be invited, be guaranteed to enjoy the right to participate with the management of industry in determining the policy of the plant concerned. That has not been done. I have here comments, statements in memoranda, every one of which agrees that all the offers of the men to cooperate with plants have been rebuffed. There has been a determination manifest on the part of industrial managers to treat the labouring men as servants, not as partners. That must be changed. It has been changed in Great Britain; it has been changed in large measure in the United States, and it must be changed in Canada.
There is one other thing which I think is rather important in this connection. May I give an illustration? Some time ago we were discussing the matter of pensions. We were discussing the Pension Act for soldiers, and a good deal of misunderstanding arose on account of the fact that we were looking only at the pensions Canadians were receiving and not at the social benefits which they were not receiving. Hon. members would rise in this chamber and say that the Pension Act of Canada grants higher pensions to men than does any other country in the world. That may possibly be. But in order properly to gauge or assess the value of the Canadian pension one must first examine and see whether or not there are other benefits to be found in other parts of the world which are not to be found in Canada. We in Canada are the most laggard nation on earth in the matter of social services. I have never heard of a modem nation anywhere that neglects the welfare of the common people as Canada does, and before I am through I shall be able to prove it. Those of us who were fortunate enough to be in the empire parliamentary group at luncheon to-day and heard Mr. Nash of New Zealand must have blushed for shame to think how pathetically inadequate was Canada's showing in comparison with what is being done in little New Zealand. If there was anyone who did not feel ashamed he must have become very callous. I desire to take only a few moments to say something about the matter of production in the aircraft industry. When I suggested yesterday afternoon that I should like to ask the minister a question or two I had no intention of keeping the minister tied up here all day, but I have been trying to ask these questions for a day or two. If I had not found an opportunity before eleven o'clock to-night probably I would have forgotten about it, because I do not like to see the minister tied down here when he has so much work to do.
Then why waste time?

I do not think it is a matter of wasting time, but the hon. member may judge for himself. I think there is some information we should have, and this is the only place where we have an opportunity of bringing certain facts to the attention of the minister. I can assure my hon. friend that I am not going to take time to make any general speech or indulge in any rhetoric.
I think to-day it is recognized by everyone, even by those of us who have no technical knowledge, that the aircraft industry has become one of the most vital industries to the winning of the war. Every battle we have lost has, in the main, been lost through lack of support in the air. The few battles we have won, Dunkirk, the Coral sea naval battle and one or two other engagements, have been won because for a time at least we had mastery of the air. For that reason the production of aircraft has become of increasing importance in the eyes of everyone who wants to see the united nations not only wun the war but win it as quickly as possible. Therefore, during the last two sessions I have been asking the minister some questions about aircraft production. He will remember that last year we discussed the question of the Malton plant, and at that time the minister said he was not very well satisfied with production there. The other evening the hon. member for Bow River said that in his opinion the aircraft factories were not working to full capacity. I do not think there should be any misunderstanding when that statement is made. There is no doubt that aircraft production in this country is much better than it was last year and that last year it was better than the year before; and any person who criticizes that production must not be understood as saying that we are not making progress. I think those responsible are making progress; but the questions I raise

This is what the editorial says:
In a letter from the Hon. C. D. Howe, Minister of Munitions and Supply, to the Port Arthur trades and labour council, we are informed that our plant has produced 726 Hawker Hurricanes to March 12, 1942, and considering the comparatively brief period during which our plant has operated we should be proud of this production record. Yet, vre, the aircraft workers cannot be proud of such a record, after thirty months of war with nazism.
We do not blame the local management for this poor production record, but vre do blame those in high places, and we state that there is something wrong in our aircraft industry, and our effort is not total war. We have not seen a great change-over from peace to total war in this country, we will agree that Canada is endeavouring to fight Hitlerism, but at the same time interfere as little as possible with the profit system and the standard practices of the controllers of industry. It is true that excess profits are heavily taxed, but the scramble for profit still goes on, and the exploitation of the great mass of workers continues as in the days of peace.
The main question of self-satisfaction will not get us anywhere, it is time all bottlenecks be removed and that the government should realize that the workers are not satisfied with present production records. Labour has already made many sacrifices in order to expedite the general war effort. This was done for two reasons: primarily because organized labour is composed of good substantial Canadians with a sense of real patriotism, and second, in an effort to show in this emergency that we stand one hundred per cent for total war, we the workers have buried the hatchet and are concentrating our efforts upon the common enemy, Hitlerism. There is a little question as to just what must be done-not to-morrow, but to-day, to do away w-ith all bottlenecks, also governments and management must realize and confess that they don't know all the answers. Invite labour to participate more fully in the readjustment to meet the war emergency, and don't hide behind

726 planes as a total war effort. We, as labour, do offer one suggestion-one that should be accepted willingly: Establish in all war industries a board of six members, three from the management ana three from labour, to be called the production board.

I wish to
make two suggestions. I cannot make suggestions along technical lines, because that is not my business. It seems to me, however, that there are two things which could be done, the first of which was mentioned to-night by the hon. member for North Battleford. It seems to me that if labour were taken into partnership to a greater extent than has been done, we would get much better production. I believe there is a great reservoir of skill and cooperation the government has not yet begun to tap. I believe the production committees in Great Britain, and the labour movements both in Australia and New Zealand are to a very great extent responsible for the wholehearted cooperation which those people have been able to give in their production effort.
When I say that, I am not casting any disparagement upon our own effort. But I do say to the minister that if labour were given the feeling that it had a voice in the councils of the nation, and that in the different shops it was sitting in with the management, planning production, offering suggestions about the removal of difficulties, and putting forth concrete recommendations for new ways and new methods, and, in some instances, providing substitutes where certain raw materials are no longer available, it might be possible to step up production much more rapidly than has been done.
The second suggestion I wish to make is one which I hope the minister will not misunderstand. From time to time it is our task to bring suggestions and even to offer criticisms of government policy. We have not always
agreed with the policies of the minister, or with some of the policies of this government. I hope the minister will never take that as meaning that we do not appreciate the work he has done for Canada. I think every hon. member-certainly every member of the group with which I am associated-has admired the minister's dynamic energy and the tireless way in which he has worked for this country. He started in with a department, from scratch, and he has built up a tremendous organization which has produced very worth-while results. That does not mean it has produced all the results it could have produced; but I should like the minister to know that, as a general rule, the Canadian people look with a great deal of favour upon his work, and are appreciative of it.
I say that because I wish to make a suggestion. The Department of Munitions and Supply has now grown to a point where in the interests of Canada's war effort it ought, in my opinion, to be divided. As has already been said, here is a department which has already placed contracts to an amount in excess of the national debt of Canada prior to the outbreak of war. In the early days when this department was being set up, probably it could be set up only in the way it was. But we have moved to the place now where it is the largest spending department in the government, larger than all the other departments put together as far as the actual placing of orders is concerned.
It seems to me that the department falls legitimately into two categories. First, it is a purchasing department, and for that reason there ought to be a separate ministry of supply charged with the responsibility of placing contracts, looking after the rationing of gasoline, rubber and many other products. These are things which ought not to be laid upon an already overworked minister, no matter how ambitious, energetic, and tireless he may be. He should not be loaded down with the purchasing, even though he may do it through subordinates, of hundreds of millions of dollars worth of commodities, all the way from boots and shoes to tanks. This is a responsibility which no one person can humanly carry.
As I say, there ought to be a ministry of supply and, on the other hand, there ought to be a ministry of production. I think the government would be well advised to turn over the whole task of placing orders and of making purchases, which has now been organized probably to a point where it is routine, to another minister and leave the present minister free to become the minister of production. He could then devote all

his drive and energy to the task of getting production. This problem is becoming more pressing. Steel has been talked about a great deal. It is not only a problem of getting steel production up to capacity; there is also the problem of whether or not the capacity can be increased.
There is now the question of getting oil. When I was home at Easter I talked to one or two men interested in the oil business and in geological surveys. They mentioned a Mr. Gower, who I believe works for the Regina Industries Limited. I do not know the gentleman, but I am told that he has spent a good deal of his own money-I believe he appeared before the national research council-working on a formula for extracting high-grade gasoline from the tar sands of Alberta. As far as I know, his formula has never been adopted. There is a whole field which ought to be investigated with a view to finding whether or not we can secure additional oil resources in Canada.
There is also the question of synthetic rubber. I believe a government-owned company, the Polymer company, has been formed, but I do not think it is anywhere near production. This is something to which a great deal of attention ought to be given. The work in this connection will have to be speeded up. Let there be a lot more drive put into it. We cannot wait six months or a year in order to get synthetic rubber. It seems to me that here is a full-time job for the best minister the government can get, and I suggest that the present Minister of Munitions and Supply should be placed in charge of production. There should be left to him the task of speeding up production if it is humanly possible in the different lines pertaining to Canada's war effort.
I make these suggestions in the best of faith. I ask the minister if everything that can be done is being done, if the complaints made by men who work in these factories have any justification in fact. I should like to ask what steps the government proposes to take in the near future to put the aircraft industry on a full-time basis in order that it may produce more of the planes without which it will be absolutely impossible for the united nations to achieve the victory we all desire.
