I may say to my hon. friend in connection with the aircraft industry that if we agreed to level off the industry and call it a day, if we said that this was our maximum objective and concentrated on reaching that objective, we could produce more planes than we are doing. The reason

why we are not producing more planes is the fact that we are constantly expanding. We have three plants that are producing nothing at the moment. They are coming in with a new type of plane and will produce eventually. I do not think we have ever stopped adding floor space to the aircraft plants. Incidental to that, we have never stopped expanding the personnel of the industry. I think every week since the war began has seen more workers in the aircraft industry than were there the previous week.
It is impossible when you are introducing new types to streamline the industry. I know my hon. friend is quite a student of production and has probably been to these plants, but I can take him to plants which he would call streamlined where every man's work is balanced against every other man's work. Every man putting in a full day's work can balance out the production of the plant. I am sorry to say that that has not been possible in the aircraft industry. There are a great number of learners in this industry, and the absorption of these learners slows down the general production. The output per man is not as great as it would be if we levelled off the industry and balanced out each man's production.
There are inequalities of that kind; nevertheless we are producing a very respectable number of planes. On the basis of comparative floor space, I would not hesitate to compare our production with that of any other country. I quite understand why people in the industry say that they are slowed down. There may be legitimate cases of that kind, but I would point out to my hon. friend that a campaign is in progress which has emerged from the country to the south. This is a campaign on the part of labour to form labour-management councils. I am not quarrelling with the objectives of that campaign; I am not quarrelling with the methods; but I say to my hon. friend that if he read the press of the United States six or seven months ago, he would have seen-the claim made that management was holding back and that the only way to cure the situation was to institute management-labour councils. That campaign has been brought over here holus-bolus and is now being carried on. I do not object to it, but I think my hon. friend, when quoting letters of that kind from labour organizations, should bear in mind that this campaign has that objective in view.

Does the
minister think that is the only objective?

War Appropriation-Supplies

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: No; I think that is the principal objective of the campaign. I do not think that fact is serious enough to warrant the publicity it has been given.

Does the
minister think they are not genuinely interested in increasing production?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I believe they are, but I think the concentration on that particular phase of the thing is too true to form. Quite often I sit down with labour groups. I sat down with one in Windsor a few days ago, and I sat down with one in the House of Commons just recently. I sit down with these groups almost every week, and the story is exactly the same. In Windsor it was the automobile industry. I hear the same thing about the aircraft industry and about the gun-making industry. As I say, the objectives of this campaign are quite legitimate and I have no objection to its succeeding. In fact, in a qhiet way I am willing to help, but I do not think it is my problem.
The aircraft industry is probably the most vulnerable for the reasons I have given. It is aD industry that is being expanded tremendously. We have orders on our books for well over 10,000 planes; I think it is more like 15,000 planes to-day. We must expand the industry farther to fill these orders. Not only is the number of planes quite high, but larger and more difficult types of planes are being produced. As my hon. friend knows, back of the industry itself, is a great multitude of plants making components which will also have to be expanded. All these parts must flow into the aircraft plant in a uniform way to bring about streamlined production.
Could the present plants work more shifts, or is there a lack of raw material?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: They can when we get levelled off, when we get uniform production. If they are working on a standard order there is an unlimited scope. Some plants are; some plants are not. For example, Noorduyn has a standardized plane and is working on a very large order. I hope that the whole industry can get on a three-shift basis in a reasonable time. But National Steel Car and de Havilland are changing to different types of planes and it is impossible for them to do it.
For the very simple reason that the companies manufacturing the component parts cannot begin to manufacture until they receive the templets.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Yes, it takes a long time to get templets made and distributed back to the
parts industry. No plane has ever been brought into production in any country in less than a year or fifteen months, and while the change is being made there is a disorganized period, finishing up odds and ends. We are now in the process of changing over to make parts for the new planes and, in such a period, production drops. The period of disorganization is longer with some managements than with others, depending upon the type of management. Some managements are more expert than others.
Canadian Car and Foundry have an order for a standardized plane?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
No. They are changing from the Hawker Hurricane to a new type of dive bomber. The production of the Hawker Hurricane is tapering off, and parts for the new dive bomber are being manufactured, but it will not be assembled as a plane that can be flown for a good many months yet. In the meantime, there will be a gradual tapering down from one kind of production, and a gradual stepping-up in the production of a totally different type of plane. That is the nature of the industry. It is not a streamlined industry such as our gun industry, where we are working four shifts a day, three shifts and a swing shift to take up the seven-day week. The tools are being worked every hour of the seven-day week. That is incidental to the gun industry.
All I can say is that we have developed good management in the aeroplane industry. My hon. friend will remember that there was no aircraft industry in this country at the beginning of the war. Every man in a management position in our aeroplane industry, with very few exceptions, is new to the industry. We had very little background in this type of industry. Nevertheless we have developed top-notch production men in the aircraft industry and top-notch designers, but they have been developed over the last two or three years. It is an industry apart. I make no great claims for it.
I will not deny that there may be people putting in time at the factory who may not be usefully employed because their section is ahead of some other section. If it was peacetime such a condition might lead to lay-offs in the aeroplane industry, but when the industry is carrying the men it can tell them frankly that their section is ahead of another section; that that is holding up the assembly, and that they had better ease down a little. That may happen. When it happens, it is not done with any idea of slowing down production as a whole or anything of that
War Appropriation-Supplies

kind. It can happen where a change-over is taking place and a new plane is coming into production.
That is what I was pointing out to the minister the other day.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I know my hon. friend knows a great deal about production, having been in it most of his life, but this time I am making a statement.
I was simply pointing out that the minister objected when I gave the very same explanation the other day.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I think I have covered the aeroplane Industry now. I am probably the goat of the industry, but I think, as the months go by, the people of Canada will be more and more pleased with the output of the industry. We could have closed the door on expansion six months ago and had a very satisfactory industry to-day, with plant on a three-shift basis and production coming out in a streamlined way, but we have tried to keep abreast with new developments in the war and take on new types of production rather than go on making planes which were becoming obsolete. We are making the changes as fast and as efficiently as we can.
My hon. friend spoke of dividing my job. I would give three cheers for that. I would like very much to have less work. But the tendency in all countries is not to divide up, but to centralize. My hon. friend has followed the progress of events in Great Britain. He knows that they have three supply ministries and that they recently appointed a ministry of production to coordinate the work of the other three branches.

Production
and supply are separate in Great Britain.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
The three supply ministries are subordinate to the minister of production, who is a coordinating officer; the same has happened in the United States. The United States had separate agencies for army and air and for the navy and for the navy air arm, and it was found that they were competing in the same factories and that there was conflict. Then the office occupied by Donald Nelson was set up as a coordinating office with complete authority over all procurement. There is a reason for that. The work of procurement and production is subdivided. But to have authority divided leads to disorganization. There is a great

advantage in having all production procurement centred in one office. My method has been to subdivide the work under me as often as it has seemed necessary, and to delegate as much work as possible. I am busy enough, it is true, but I do not know that I am doing more work than a good many other people in this country. I can say to my hon. friend that the reason why the work of procurement is not divided is that it would mean a loss of efficiency.
I thank the minister for the explanation he has given. I appreciate it very much, but he did not have to intimate that I was a student of production. He was either pulling my leg or being sarcastic.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: My hon. friend was very nice to me, and I thought I would be very nice to him.

I did not appreciate his either pulling my leg or, being sarcastic. The explanation given by the minister is the kind of statement which, it seems to me, does serve a useful purpose because when the men in these plants are not being utilized to the full, the impression gets around that this thing is a racket. That is how they talk, and some explanation of why they are idle ought to be forthcoming. I do not know anything about production, it is true, because a member of this house cannot be a student of everything that comes within the departments of all the ministers, but it is the duty of a member of this house to bring these matters to the attention of the minister so that he can make the kind of statement he made to-night. I do not think the minister ought to pull anybody's leg or be sarcastic about members being students of production all their lives.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I did not intend any sarcasm. My hon. friend has shown a great interest in production.
The sarcasm was intended for me.

I did not take any offence. I want to thank the minister again for his statement, and if statements of that kind were made more often it would be of great value to the country. The explanation is that there is a tapering-off from one type of production so that the plant can move into the production of another type of plane because some of the older types have become obsolete. But in the case which the minister mentioned at Fort William, that is a plane which, I understand, is still in use-the Hawker Hurricane.

War Appropriation-Supplies

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Yes.

What is the object in making a switch there? Men who have done some reading along the line of aircraft production say that one of the things that got Great Britain off to a bad start before the war was the fact that, whereas Goering went into mass production of Messerschmitts and probably produced inferior planes but produced them on a standard line, the British constantly kept changing their designs, which meant long periods of delay. Is there a danger of us doing that here? Is a lot of this switching necessary? Is it necessary to be constantly changing some of the types? Are we reducing the number of types and trying to get down to two or three standard lines which could be produced on a steady basis, rather than making these constant switches which, as the minister has said, must entail periods of non-production?
That is the first change which has been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: The reason why we are leaving the Hawker Hurricane for another plane is that our air force demands the best and the Hurricane is getting out of date. To-day there are much better fighting planes, faster and more manoeuverable planes, than the Hurricane, and I think it is desirable not to maintain in production an obsolescent type. It is true that far more planes would have been produced by this time if the British had kept to pre-war types, but I would point out that by getting more advanced types they have gained control of the air, and gained it at a time when they undoubtedly had fewer planes than the enemy. I certainly have to accept the judgment of the operational forces as to the type of planes which we should produce.

I have a question to ask regarding the manufacture of steel. We know that steel is in great demand these days. The last time I visited Trail smelters I noticed they had a mountain of what looked like good material if it were smelted down and perhaps manufactured into steel. This was the residue from their mining operations. I do not know how many tons would be there, but it seems to me that the mountain they had was about a mile long. Has the minister had any report regarding the great mountain which they have there and which I believe they are willing shall be used?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I have no report on it, but I think there would be transportation difficulties in the way. The equipment necessary to turn ore into steel is very rare. We have
only three places in Canada with sufficient equipment to take ore of any kind and make finished steel from it-Sault Ste. Marie, Hamilton and Sydney, Nova Scotia. While I have no knowledge of this particular situation, I assume the transportation difficulty is there.
I will, however, make inquiries.
I believe that it is worth looking into. I am under the impression that it could be smelted there, and there is sufficient to warrant the installation of a small smelter.

In Great Britain they
design planes. Their engineers design a new plane from experience of their pilots in the air in opposition to planes which have been designed in Germany or elsewhere. In the United States also they design planes. In Canada we do not do any designing; we make only what has been proved to be satisfactory in Great Britain. Is that not one of the main differences between conditions of aircraft manufacture in Canada and Great Britain? So, when we undertake to make a type of plane which has been proved to be satisfactory in Britain, our companies first have to make their blue prints, of which there may be 20,000 or 25,000 for one new design; then they have to adjust their tools to suit that work, or retool, and arrange for all the component parts involved in the new design. But we do not really design any new plane in Canada in the sense that they do in England-for instance, a Lancaster. *

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Please do not mention the names of new planes. We do design in Canada a Fleet-60 which is used for advanced training by the air force. We have designed some very important modifications of planes, but of course the designing industry is new in Canada as it is elsewhere. We have brilliant designers, but they have not the background of experience which is possessed by designers in either the United States or Great Britain. Designing talent is improving month by month, and I think that if occasion calls for the designing of a new type of plane in Canada, we have people here who are competent to do it. I may say, however, that when we take a British or even a United States design, but especially the former, there is a good deal of redesigning to do to fit Canadian methods. We here are fairly well advanced in mass production, and our methods are different from those in the old country. So we have quite an engineering department in our aircraft industry.

What I meant was the
new planes.
War Appropriation-Supplies

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: The Fleet-60 is, I think, the only case of a new plane which was completely designed in Canada.

It has been brought to my attention that in some cases where contracts have been given for aeroplane construction, for example, where the government would place a contract for, say twenty-five planes with a company, the plant would get tooled up for that work, and they have represented that they could have made thirty-five planes just as easily-I am using this number as an illustration-in practically the same length of time, but their instruction was to make twenty-five planes and they could not go ahead any faster than that limited order would permit. If, however, the order had been increased they could have manufactured quite a number of additional planes in the same period.
One other point. In the minister's remarks a while ago I think he stated-I am not arguing the point with him-that in some departments of a factory it was possible that the management would require the workers to slow up a little bit. I think that is a fair interpretation of what he said, and it bears out exactly what I was trying to tell the minister the other day, that in some of those places the fellows have come to me and told me they were requested not to do so much work.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: But the implication my hon. friend drew was that they were trying to slow down production of the finished article- which is not the case.

Whether that was the final result or not is not the point I am now discussing. The point is that these people were deliberately advised to slow down. They came to me as a member of parliament and objected to that, and I think they were perfectly right in doing so. The minister now admits it would be possible in some instances that the management would go to these fellows and say to them that they might not have to work very fast, that if they did they would run out of a job.
Would the minister straighten up the question I asked him about the limited number in a contract? Would these companies be allowed to make five or ten planes more if they could, if they had the material?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
When my hon. friend speaks af twenty or twenty-five planes he is talking about pre-war days. Planes to-day are built certainly in the hundreds; I do not know of any contract for less than two hundred that
[Mr. MacNicol.j
has been placed in the last two years. However, we do build planes to meet a demand. Sometimes we build them without knowing exactly who wants them, if they are a plane in common use. But in pre-war days we used to tool up to make ten or fifteen or twenty planes, when the industry was very small. To-day we place large orders. Any factory that is in production to-day is either working on an unlimited order or is tooling up to make planes for which it will have an unlimited order. Therefore my hon. friend's question is hardly pertinent to the present-day situation.
If they are working on a limited order will they be allowed to go over that?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: It would depend on whether we thought we could get rid of the planes. We would have to find a use for the planes. We are not flyers ourselves and we do not want the planes to rust. The Hurricane plant at Fort William had an order for 600 Hurricanes; they were coming to the end of the order and I told them to make 400 more. I did not know al the time what do with them, but since then I have found uses for them and now the plant are unlimited in the sense that they can make all the Hurricanes they can until the new plane comes into production. That is the usual situation in our plants to-day. Fairchild has all the work it can do until the end of 1943 and Nooduyn until the end of 1944. These might be called unlimited orders.
That is the way it should be.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: That is the way it is. Nevertheless, we do get modifications. For instance, there may be modifications interjected into a programme which might slow the plant down for a month or two. That is incidental to war. If actual experience indicates that better results can be obtained through a modification, we have to stop the production line and make the modification; but of course we appreciate the desirability of working without interruption, and we are as anxious to do this as my hon. friend is to have us do it.
If you are on an unlimited order for Hurricanes, could you not get greater production? Is it a matter of trained personnel?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: It is a matter of both supervision and trained personnel and organizing the shops behind the assembly plants to feed the material in.

Are you making any torpedo-carrying planes?

Labour Conditions

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Yes; we are coming into production.

Is anything being done with regard to duplicating oil pipelines from Oklahoma to Sarnia? I do not quite understand why the notification has been given about no oil for homes. I do not know why it has come so suddenly seeing that a month ago we were told that heating for homes would be all right. Two months ago, I know, several buildings in Toronto were notified to put coal in. I was wondering if something had suddenly happened in the central provinces to make the difference.
Has the minister's department done anything in connection with the study of camouflage for factories and so on, as they are doing in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: We are not building pipelines at the moment. With regard to oil, I was asked a question in the house and I gave an answer which I wish to amplify. Our study of the situation has not been quite completed. There is no doubt in the world that those who have converted coal furnaces into oil burners will be required to convert them back to coal. For the furnace which has been put in as an oil furnace, and which cannot be converted except by removing the furnace and putting in a new furnace, we will, I think, endeavour to find a supply, for the reason that it is not practical to build furnaces and supply them under such circumstances. Here again, every hon. member knows that the oil situation is extremely critical. The best I can say is that a complete statement will be made on the whole fuel situation for next winter in the course of a week or two. In the meantime I should like to amplify the statement I made yesterday to that extent, that an effort will . be made to supply the oil installation which cannot be converted to coal.
Will that rule apply to the ferryboat serving between the mainland and Prince Edward Island? It is only within recent months that there was a change over from coal to oil.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
The reason why that was
done is that it is impossible and always has been impossible to keep up steam with a coal-fire boiler when that boat is working in the ice. It was changed to oil as a measure of security having regard to the fact that there is no standby for this ferry. I do not wish to speak finally on that, but that might be one of the cases where the use of oil as fuel would be considered imperative for the sake of safety. That again is the subject of investigation.	*
As regards the question of camouflage, we are camouflaging key plants in areas that are regarded by the military authorities as dangerous. That work is going on at the present time.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, May 22, 1942
